sens: horizontal piece of wood on a loom, on which the threads are wound
shaft or pole of a spear compared to this piece of wood by its size and shape
H4500.detail: 1. In a loom, the ensouple is the large round or cylindrical piece of wood on which the warp threads are wound. It is thick, solid, and regular, as required by its role of support and tension. 2. In warrior passages, the ensouple of the weaver becomes an image to describe the shaft of certain spears: it is said that the wood of the spear was thick and heavy "like a weaver's ensouple." This comparison is striking in its detail — it is the most vivid way to show that it was not an ordinary weapon, but a massive and impressive spear. In 1 Samuel 17:7, Goliath's spear has its shaft described this way, and in 1 Chronicles 11:23, the Egyptian that Benaiah faced carried a similar spear.
H4500.origine: The Hebrew word מָנוֹר (manor) literally refers to the roll or piece of wood of the loom. There is no apparent link with other biblical roots; the term remains specialized in the field of weaving. It is a technical word from the artisanal world of the time.
H4500.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe the shaft of the great spears of the adversaries of the Israelites: that of Goliath (1 Samuel 17:7), that of the Egyptian killed by Benaiah (1 Chronicles 11:23), and that of Goliath's brother (2 Samuel 21:19 and 1 Chronicles 20:5). The repetition of this same comparison emphasizes the extraordinary size and impressive solidity of these weapons, thereby highlighting the courage or superhuman power of those who wield them.
H4500.portee: This word reminds us that Scripture speaks of the visible, concrete, and technical world: a loom, a spear. The comparison with the ensouple makes the scene tangible and vivid. It also helps us measure the challenge posed by these giants and their weapons — Goliath was not a vague threat, but a crushing material reality. It magnifies by contrast the miracle of faith when David, armed only with his sling, confronts this mountain of flesh and steel.

sens: Liturgical furniture carrying lamps, in the tabernacle and the temple
Set of branches carrying the lamps
Each of the individual branches of the chandelier
H4501.detail:
1. The chandelier is a special piece of furniture used in the worship of Israel to illuminate the sanctuary. It was placed inside the tabernacle or the temple, facing the table of showbread (Exodus 26:35), and its lamps were to burn continuously to light the holy place (Leviticus 24:4).

2. The chandelier consists of a central shaft and six lateral branches that extend from it, three on each side (Exodus 37:18). This set formed a unique structure, crafted from pure gold in one piece (Exodus 25:31), decorated with knobs and flowers.

3. Each of the branches of the chandelier was also called a "chandelier": they each held a lamp, and holy oils were poured into them (Numbers 8:2-3), so that the word designated sometimes the entire device, sometimes each of its luminous elements.
H4501.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to illuminate." It is a typically Israelite object, created according to the divine revelation given to Moses on Mount Sinai. In Solomon's temple, several examples were found: Solomon made ten of gold (2 Chronicles 4:7), while Exodus describes only one for the tabernacle.
H4501.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Bible, mainly in the books of Exodus, Numbers, Chronicles, and Zechariah. It describes the meticulous construction of the chandelier according to divine instructions (Exodus 25, 37), the placement of the furniture in the sanctuary (Exodus 40:24), the daily maintenance of its lamps (Numbers 8:3), and the multiple chandeliers of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 4:7). Zechariah also mentions the chandelier in a prophetic vision (Zechariah 4:2-11), symbolizing the people or the Spirit of God.
H4501.portee: The chandelier reminds us that God dwells in light and that He asks His people to keep the light of the sanctuary alive. It is an image of the divine presence and the necessity of continual service. For the Christian, it prefigures Jesus Christ, the light of the world, and reminds us that we are called to be like lamps that shine to glorify God.

sens: Leader or high-ranking individual
One who has authority and power
Figure of dignity and command
H4502.detail:
1. The word designates a leader or an individual endowed with authority: it is someone who exercises power and directs. In Nahum 3:17, God compares the princes of the Assyrian kingdom to locusts that fly away: the image suggests the instability and fragility of those who seemed powerful.

2. It is also one who has the dignity and prestige attached to a high rank. However, the biblical text highlights that this apparent greatness can be quickly annihilated: princes are not exempt from divine judgment.

3. The word can evoke one who is consecrated or distinguished, possessing a form of special status in society. But the vulnerability of the Assyrian prince in the face of ruin shows that human rank, no matter how high, does not guarantee protection against downfall.
H4502.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of distinction or separation: one who is set apart, elevated above others. The exact meaning remains partially obscure to specialists, but the biblical context associates it with a function of command and authority. This term fits within the vocabulary of the social and political hierarchy of the ancient Near East.
H4502.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 3:17. God speaks through the prophet Nahum to announce the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, this feared power. The princes of this nation, despite all their authority and number, are compared to defenseless locusts: they will disappear when the sun rises, that is, when God's judgment is executed. The unique use of the word places it at the heart of a prophecy of destruction, emphasizing how even the greatest cannot escape the divine plan.
H4502.portee: This text teaches the believer that human power, no matter how impressive, does not withstand the justice of God. The Assyrian princes, with all their appearance of strength and multitude, prove to be as fragile as insects. This invites the reader to place their trust not in earthly powers, but in God who overturns empires. The lesson remains current: no human dignity or authority is above divine will.

sens: Gift or present offered to someone to honor or satisfy them
Tribute paid to a king or superior
Sacrifice or gift brought to God, especially from the products of the land
H4503G.detail:
1. In the broadest sense, an offering is a gift presented to someone to gratify or pay homage to them (Genesis 4:3, where Cain brings an offering of the fruits of the land to the Lord).

2. It can be a tribute or contribution owed to a king or authority, a form of recognition and submission.

3. In Israel's worship, the offering primarily becomes a plant sacrifice brought to the Lord: fine flour mixed with oil, grains, or other products of the land (Leviticus 2:1-15). Unlike the burnt offering, which is completely consumed, the offering is shared between the altar and the priests (Leviticus 7:10). It often accompanies other sacrifices (Numbers 29:11).
H4503G.origine: The Hebrew word מִנְחָה (minha) comes from a root meaning "to present" or "to give." Its primitive meaning is that of a voluntary gift, a present given face to face. In the Law, this word specifically refers to the offering of flour and oil, a part of the Israelite sacrificial system. The Greek word θυσία (thysia, sacrifice) often translates it, but וְנָחַם (menuhah) and מִנְחָה have distinct nuances.
H4503G.emploi: The word offering appears 160 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the legislative books (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers). In the early accounts, it refers to gifts brought to God (Cain in Genesis 4:3-5, the princes of Israel in Numbers 7). In the Mosaic Law, it takes on a technical meaning: it is the plant sacrifice of chapter 2 of Leviticus, made of fine flour, oil, and incense. This sacrifice appears daily in worship and during festivals (Numbers 28-29). It can be brought alongside other sacrifices or for atonement (Leviticus 5:13). The offering affirms Israel's dependence on God and acknowledges His lordship through a material gift.
H4503G.portee: The offering shows that serving God is not limited to obeying out of fear: it is also about voluntarily presenting what we possess, recognizing that He is our Lord and that everything comes from Him. The Christian sees it as a type of Christ's perfect offering, who presented Himself to God as a pleasing aroma (Ephesians 5:2). It invites us to give to God not out of legal obligation, but out of love and gratitude.

sens: Gift offered to someone to honor or win their favor
Tribute or gift given to a king or a powerful person
Offering brought to the Lord
H4503H.detail:
1. It is primarily a gift made to someone to honor them or obtain their goodwill. Jacob prepares one for Esau (Genesis 32:13) to appease his anger. It is a gesture of respect and reconciliation: the presents travel ahead of Jacob before his meeting with his brother (Genesis 32:21).
2. It is also a tribute paid to a king or a powerful person, a gift-tax that acknowledges their authority. When kings visit each other or pay court to a powerful monarch, each brings their present (2 Chronicles 9:24). Hazael brings a present to the prophet Elisha as one would to a king (2 Kings 8:8).
3. Finally, it is an offering presented to God, a sacrifice or oblation. Gideon prepares an offering for the Lord, which he lays before Him (Judges 6:18), thus acknowledging divine sovereignty as one would do to a king.
H4503H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "gift" or "present." It first designates any gift or tribute, then naturally applies to offerings made to God, as offering to God is treating Him as a king who deserves all honors.
H4503H.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Bible, mainly in the Old Testament. It primarily refers to political or diplomatic presents between kings and powerful individuals (2 Kings 8:8-9; 2 Chronicles 9:24). Jacob and his sons use it to speak of the gifts they offer (Genesis 32-43). The religious usage is particularly found in Judges 6:18 when Gideon offers an offering to the Lord. The word thus covers a wide spectrum: from simple gifts to royal tributes, then to sacred offerings.
H4503H.portee: This word shows how the Bible conceives the relationship with God: we honor Him as we honor a king, by presenting Him gifts. It is a way of recognizing His greatness and sovereignty. For the Christian, it invites reflection on the meaning of sacrifice and offering in the relationship with God.

sens: Gift, present offered to someone
Tax or fee imposed on a conquered or subdued people
Offering presented to God
H4503I.detail:
1. The word first designates a gift or present offered to someone, often to honor them or obtain their favor. Ehud brings a present to Eglon, king of Moab (Judges 3:15), and it is specified that he "finished offering the present" (Judges 3:18). It is a gesture of respect or submission.
2. The tribute is also the tax or fee that a conquered people must pay or that is imposed on them. After David defeated the Moabites, "the Moabites became subject to David and paid him tribute" (1 Chronicles 18:2). Similarly, the Syrians "became subject to David, and paid him tribute" (2 Samuel 8:6). It is an obligation imposed on the defeated.
3. The word also applies to offerings presented to God: faithful kings receive presents from their subjects (2 Chronicles 17:5). This meaning aligns with the idea of an offering rendered in recognition of authority or blessing.
H4503I.origine: The Hebrew word min.chah comes from a root meaning "to give" or "to present." It is related to the idea of making a gesture of offering or submission to someone more powerful. In the context of Israelite worship, the word specifically refers to the grain offering (the plant offering) presented to the Lord, distinct from the animal sacrifice. The central notion is that of a voluntary or obligatory presentation to one who holds authority.
H4503I.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). It is used to describe diplomatic presents between kings (Judges 3:15: Ehud brings a present to Eglon), the tributes demanded from conquered peoples (2 Samuel 8:6; 1 Chronicles 18:2), and the presents brought by subjects to their king (2 Chronicles 17:5). The context varies: sometimes it is a humiliating act (tribute to the victors), sometimes an act of respect or allegiance. In a few cases, the word applies to the religious offering to God, particularly the grain offering.
H4503I.portee: This word reminds the believer that every offering—whether a gift, tribute, or presentation to God—expresses a recognition of the authority of the one receiving it. For Israel, bringing tribute to a foreign king was a mark of subjection; bringing an offering to the Lord was, on the contrary, an act of freedom and worship. Understanding this distinction helps the believer grasp what it truly means to present oneself before God: not out of forced obligation, but out of joyful recognition of His authority and benevolence.

sens: Gift given to God or a king as a sign of respect and submission
Sacrifice or offering brought to the altar of the temple
Material gift offered to someone in a position of authority
H4504.detail:
1. An offering is a gift given to God or a king to show respect and submission. It is a concrete act of veneration: it acknowledges the authority and greatness of the one who receives it. When King Nebuchadnezzar bows down before Daniel, he orders that sacrifices and incense be offered to him — it is an offering to one he has just recognized as superior (Daniel 2:46).

2. An offering can be a sacrifice brought to the altar of the temple, an essential part of the worship rendered to God. In the law of Israel, the offering included bulls, rams, and lambs, intended to be presented to God in Jerusalem to obtain His favor or to atone for sins (Ezra 7:17).

3. More broadly, it is any material gift offered respectfully to someone: food, animals, incense, or another present depending on the context and the recipient.
H4504.origine: The Hebrew word מִנְחָה (minchah) comes from a root that means "to give" or "to present." It essentially designates what is brought or presented — first to God, then to any high-ranking individual. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often corresponds to the term "offering" or "gift." The offering was a central act of Israelite worship, expressing the people's acknowledgment of God.
H4504.emploi: This word appears 2 times in the provided Segond. In Ezra 7:17, it refers to a sacrificial offering at the temple: Ezra must buy with money the animals and what is needed for the offerings and libations at the altar. In Daniel 2:46, when King Nebuchadnezzar bows down before Daniel, he orders that sacrifices and incense be offered to him — an offering to a man recognized as having supernatural wisdom. Thus, the offering expresses respect and acknowledgment toward the one to whom it is presented, whether God or a representative of divine authority.
H4504.portee: The offering reminds the believer that the relationship with God or with established authority is based on voluntary and respectful giving. It teaches us that recognizing someone's greatness means being willing to offer something of oneself or one's possessions. For the Christian, this principle resonates with the call to offer one's entire life to God: not out of obligation, but as a sign of love and submission.

sens: King of the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the time of the Divided Monarchy
Son of Gadi and father of Pekahiah
Contemporary of the prophets Hosea and Amos
Ruler who reigned for ten years by force and subjected Israel to Assyrian tribute
H4505.detail: Menahem is a king of Israel (the Northern Kingdom) who lived during the time when the Hebrew people were divided into two rival kingdoms. He is the son of Gadi and the father of Pekahiah, who continued his royal lineage. His name means "the one who comforts" in Hebrew, which sharply contrasts with his brutal reign: he took the throne by killing Shallum, a usurper, and reigned for ten years in Samaria. He was a powerful but ruthless king, as shown by his attack on Tiphsach (2 Kings 15:16), where he had pregnant women disemboweled because the city refused to open its gates to him. A contemporary of the prophets Hosea and Amos, who preached against the sins of Israel, Menahem held the throne with an iron fist: he imposed a heavy tribute of silver on all the wealthy of Israel (2 Kings 15:20) to pay King Pul of Assyria, to whom he submitted to strengthen his power (2 Kings 15:19). His reign illustrates both the political strength and moral corruption of the last kings of the North.
H4505.origine: The name Menahem comes from the Hebrew root that means "to comfort" or "to console." This prophetic name contrasts with the historical reality of a reign marked by violence and oppression. It is part of the royal family of the North, in the long succession of rulers who dominated the divided kingdom.
H4505.emploi: Menahem appears eight times in the biblical text, exclusively in the account of his reign in 2 Kings 15:14-23. The biblical sources first present him as the son of Gadi who came up from the south to Samaria to overthrow the usurper Shallum (2 Kings 15:14). They then highlight his brutality: his attacks against Tiphsach and his violent reactions against those who resisted. They recount his ten-year reign in Samaria, his submission to Assyrian tribute, and how he imposed heavy taxation on the people to pay Assyria. The biblical account classifies him among the kings of the North who did evil in the sight of the Lord, without God intervening to correct him in these last years of the kingdom before its fall.
H4505.portee: The reign of Menahem reminds us how political power, even when strong, does not guarantee stability or the favor of God. His onomastic irony — a king named "comforter" who terrorizes his people — illustrates the gap between the name and the deeds. For the Christian reader, Menahem exemplifies how pride and violence in leadership lead to the forgetting of God and to servitude: his submission to Assyrian tribute foreshadows the decline of the Northern kingdom.

sens: place in Benjamin where some inhabitants were deported
H4506A.detail: Manachath is a location situated in the territory of Benjamin. According to 1 Chronicles 8:6, family leaders from Gibeah were transported there. The name literally means "rest" or "quiet dwelling," evoking a refuge or a place of settlement.
H4506A.origine: The Hebrew name comes from the root נוח (nuakh), which means "to rest" or "to settle." This same root is found in the name מְנוּחָה (Menukhah, "Nohah"), another designation for the place. The initial image is that of rest after movement, the calm that follows wandering.
H4506A.emploi: Manachath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:6. This passage lists the descendants of Ehud, family leaders among the inhabitants of Gibeah. These families were transported to Manachath, which seems to indicate either deportation or organized migration. The genealogical context shows that this place was known and significant for the tribes of the northern territory of Benjamin.

sens: Man living in the time of the Patriarchs, son of Shobal and descendant of Seir the Horite
H4506B.detail: Manahath is a minor character in the genealogy of the Horites, of whom Scripture reports no particular deeds. He appears in two identical genealogical lists: Genesis 36:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:40, where he is listed as one of the sons of Shobal, alongside Alvan, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. His name means "rest" in Hebrew. A descendant of Seir the Horite, he is part of the indigenous peoples of Canaan before the arrival of the Israelites.
H4506B.origine: The name Manahath (מָנַ֫חַת) literally means "rest" or "place of rest." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of settling down, finding rest. This name was borne during the patriarchal era in the lineages of the peoples of Canaan, notably among the Horites.
H4506B.emploi: Manahath is mentioned only twice in Scripture, both times in genealogical context: first in Genesis 36:23 as the son of Shobal, and a second time in 1 Chronicles 1:40, in a repetition of the same genealogy. No event is associated with him: the Bible mentions him only to establish the lines of descent of the pre-Israelite peoples of Canaan.

sens: Group of descendants of Manahath, a man from the patriarchal era
H4506G.detail: 1. The Hatsi-Hammanachthi are a clan or group of descendants from Manahath, a man who lived during the time of the Patriarchs. Manahath was the son of Shobal, who was himself the son of Seir the Horite, an ancient lineage from Canaan. In 1 Chronicles 2:54, this group is mentioned alongside other families of Judah, indicating that it was an established population in Judea, with its own traditions and identity.
H4506G.origine: The name comes from Manahath, which means "rest." Manahath is an eponymous ancestor: the group bears his name to mark its descent. The lineage traces back to Shobal and Seir the Horite, figures from the Old Testament associated with the peoples of Canaan before the Israelite conquest.
H4506G.emploi: The term appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:54, where it is listed in the genealogy of Judah. It is mentioned in a list of clans or families associated with the region of Bethlehem and its surroundings, alongside the Nethophathites, the Athroth-Beth-Joab, and the Tsoreites. This mention shows that the Hatsi-Hammanachthi constituted a recognized and established group in Judea, although few details are given about their history or role.

sens: Name of a people or family from ancient Israel
H4506H.detail: Manachath refers to a group or family about which very little is known. The Bible mentions it only once, in 1 Chronicles 2:52, where it is presented as a descendant of Shobal, who himself was from Seir the Horite. This genealogical connection suggests ancient ties with the populations of the Edom region or its surroundings.
H4506H.origine: The name Manachath is likely related to a root meaning "rest" or "stable dwelling." It appears in genealogical lists tracing the families of the primitive inhabitants of the territory. Its unique appearance in the preserved biblical texts makes it a rare element of genealogical traditions.
H4506H.emploi: Manachath appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:52, where it is listed among the descendants of Shobal. This passage is part of the larger genealogy of Judah and neighboring peoples, documenting the families that inhabited the region before or during the establishment of Israel. Its uniqueness in the biblical text makes it an almost forgotten mention in ancient genealogical records.

sens: Deity of fate worshiped by the Israelites in exile
H4507.detail: Méni is the name of a foreign deity, that of fate or fortune, which some Israelites worshiped during their exile in Babylon. The prophet Isaiah harshly criticizes this practice in Isaiah 65:11, where he reproaches the unfaithful for "preparing a table for Méni," an expression that evokes a cult performed with offerings.
H4507.origine: The name Méni comes from a Semitic root meaning "part" or "portion" (that which fate assigns to each). It is a Babylonian deity, not a God of Israel: the exiled Israelites borrowed this worship from their neighbors.
H4507.emploi: Méni appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 65:11. The context is an oracle from the Lord denouncing the unfaithful Israelites: they have turned their backs on the true God to serve foreign gods. Isaiah mentions Méni alongside another deity (Gad), emphasizing that the apostasy of the exiles extended to multiple pagan cults.
H4507.portee: This passage reminds the people of God that turning away from the Lord to seek salvation elsewhere — whether in impersonal fate or in worldly powers — is a serious unfaithfulness. It is an invitation to return to the living God rather than relying on the false gods of the time.

sens: region of ancient Armenia
H4508.detail: Minni is a mountainous region of Armenia, mentioned only once in the Bible as one of the powers that God calls to fight against Babylon. Its name might mean "division," perhaps referring to the valleys and divided regions of this mountainous land. In Jeremiah 51:27, the prophet lists three allies called to the assault: Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, three warrior peoples from the north.
H4508.origine: The name Minni historically designates a region of the Armenian plateau, known to the ancient Assyrians and Babylonians who mentioned it in their annals. Its etymology suggests the idea of division or sharing, which corresponds to the rugged geography of Armenia. This term belongs to the vocabulary of the peoples and regions of the ancient Near East.
H4508.emploi: Minni appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 51:27. The prophet Jeremiah enumerates the nations that the Lord will raise against Babylon to punish it. Minni is listed alongside Ararat and Ashkenaz as a military power from the north called to this divine vengeance. This passage situates Minni within the context of the great empires and kingdoms of the Near East surrounding Babylon.

sens: Levite during the reign of King Hezekiah
H4509G.detail: 1. Minjamin is a Levite who lived during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah. He is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 31:15 as one of the officials responsible for distributing food to the priests and Levites in the priestly cities, working under the supervision of a chief. His role shows that even in the administration of worship in Jerusalem, reliable Levites were designated to manage the goods intended for temple service.
H4509G.origine: The name Minjamin literally means "of the right hand" in Hebrew (from the root יָמִין yamin, "right hand"). This name evokes either a blessing (the right hand is a symbol of strength and favor) or a position of trust and responsibility. The name was also borne by a priest during the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem at the time of Nehemiah, although the two individuals are likely not the same.
H4509G.emploi: Minjamin is mentioned only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:15. He is found among the Levites responsible for distributing food to the priests and Levites in the priestly cities, at the time when King Hezekiah had organized a great reform of worship. His name appears in a list of faithful executors tasked with ensuring that everyone received their fair share, "both great and small, according to their divisions."

sens: Priest during the time of Nehemiah
Levite during the reign of Hezekiah
H4509H.detail:
1. Minjamin is a priest who participates in the great ceremony of dedicating the wall of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah, around the middle of the 5th century BC. He is mentioned alongside other priests, holding a trumpet to celebrate this crucial event of the return from exile (Nehemiah 12:41).
2. According to some traditions, the name Minjamin also refers to a Levite during the time of King Hezekiah, although this latter is not explicitly attested in the preserved usages.
H4509H.origine: The name Minjamin literally means "of the right hand" or "from the right side," composed of the preposition min ("of") and the Hebrew yamin ("right"). This name evokes the right side as a symbol of strength and favor in biblical culture. It is a name borne by members of the Levitical and priestly community during the return from exile.
H4509H.emploi: Minjamin appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:41, where he is named among the priests participating in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem. This ceremony, described in Nehemiah 12, gathers the chief priests to celebrate the completion of the restoration work of the city. Minjamin, holding a trumpet, is among the officiants who praise God during this decisive moment for the Jewish community returned from exile.

sens: Levite during the time of Nehemiah
H4509I.detail: Minjamin is a Levite mentioned during the time of Nehemiah, during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He appears in the list of priests and Levites who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:17).
H4509I.origine: The name Minjamin means "of the right hand" or "descendant of the right." It comes from the Hebrew root that evokes what is on the right, a symbol of strength, power, and blessing in biblical culture. This same name or an analogous variant (Mijamin) designates other figures from biblical antiquity.
H4509I.emploi: Minjamin is a Levite who lived during the time of Nehemiah, after the return from the Babylonian exile (around the 5th century BC). He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:17, among the priests and Levites present at the solemn ceremony of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem. This participation shows his active role in the religious and material restoration of the Jewish community after the exile.

sens: Total counted of objects or people
Determined quantity, enumeration
Numerical value, figure
H4510.detail:
1. The number primarily designates the totality of objects or people that can be counted together. Here, the twelve goats offered in sacrifice correspond to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel: each tribe is represented by a goat.

2. It is also the result of an enumeration, a quantity that has been counted. When the sacrifices offered at the dedication of the temple are listed — one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs — they are organized by number, meaning they are classified and counted.

3. More broadly, the number is the notion of quantity itself, the idea that something can be counted, measured, ordered.
H4510.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root that means "to count" or "to fix." It is related to other Hebrew and Aramaic forms linked to the action of counting, enumerating, or fixing a duration. The underlying notion is one of order and determination: the number brings order to a multitude.
H4510.emploi: The word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament of the provided biblical text, in Ezra 6:17, where it specifies the sacrifices offered for the dedication of the second temple. In this context, the number serves to correspond the expiatory victims — the twelve goats — to the twelve tribes of Israel. It is a way of showing that all Israel, represented by its tribes, is included in this act of reconciliation. The word thus expresses both the idea of counted quantity and that of order, correspondence.
H4510.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God loves order and precision in worship. No detail is left to chance: each sacrifice has its number, each tribe its representation. This also shows that in God's plan, nothing escapes His attention and accounting: He knows and counts His people.

sens: city located east of the Jordan in Ammonite territory
region known for its agricultural products, especially wheat
H4511.detail:
1. Minnith is a city in the Ammonite region, east of the Jordan. It appears in the account of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites: divine judgment extends "from Aroer to Minnith," encompassing twenty cities (Judges 11:33). It was therefore an important locality in enemy territory.
2. Minnith was famous for its agricultural products, particularly quality wheat. Ezekiel mentions it among the goods that Judah and Israel exported to Tyre: "the wheat of Minnith, the pastry, the honey, the oil, and the balm" (Ezekiel 27:17). This shows that this region was prosperous and its crops renowned.
H4511.origine: The name means "distribution" or "sharing," perhaps referring to how lands or harvests were administered there. The Hebrew word מִנִּית reflects a territorial organization. The locality is exclusively attested in these two biblical passages.
H4511.emploi: Minnith appears twice in the Bible. First in Judges 11:33, where it marks the northern limit of Jephthah's victorious campaign against the Ammonites, confirming its strategic importance in enemy territory. Then in Ezekiel 27:17, in the catalog of commercial goods of Tyre, where it represents the land of Israel and Judah as exporters of wheat and food products. These two passages reveal Minnith as a city that is both militarily significant and economically prosperous.

sens: acquired good or wealth
possession obtained through work or effort
H4512.detail:
1. The word designates goods, wealth, or what one has acquired — the gain derived from one's activity. In Job 15:29, Bildad speaks of a man whose "wealth will not be stable" (literal translation of the context): it refers to the material possessions one accumulates.
2. More broadly, it encompasses everything one obtains or possesses as personal property, whether earned through work, inheritance, or savings. The word carries the idea of acquisition, of something that has been gradually gathered.
H4512.origine: The word comes from a root that refers to the idea of taking, seizing, or acquiring. The exact meaning of the Hebrew term remains partially uncertain in ancient lexicons, but the biblical context and related words point towards the accumulation of material goods and wealth.
H4512.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 15:29. Bildad the Shuhite uses it to describe the material wealth of a wicked man who believes he is safe from ruin. This unique usage suggests that the word belongs to a poetic or refined vocabulary, characteristic of the book of Job where rare terms abound. The context of Bildad's speech — a debate on the fate of the wicked — shows that this gain or wealth is presented as unstable and destined to disappear.
H4512.portee: This word reminds us that material wealth is fragile and temporary. In Bildad's mouth, it illustrates an important biblical truth: accumulating goods without seeking God is vain, for these possessions will not last. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to place one's heart in earthly acquisitions, but in what has eternal value.

sens: Not giving, not granting what one could or should give
Preventing someone from doing or having something
Withholding, keeping for oneself what one should share
Diverting, dissuading someone from an action
H4513.detail:
1. To refuse primarily means not to give what is requested or what should be given. Psalm 21:3 shows the opposite: God did not refuse what the lips of the king requested, meaning He granted his requests. It is the act of saying no, of not consenting.

2. To prevent someone means to forbid them access to something, to block their way. In Genesis 30:2, Jacob asks Rachel: "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?" — only God can prevent her from having children. It is to block the path, to create an obstacle.

3. To withhold is to keep for oneself what one should share or give. Proverbs 11:26 condemns the one who withholds grain: he is cursed because he hides food while others are hungry. It is a voluntary deprivation inflicted on others.

4. To divert someone means to steer them away from an action, to dissuade them. In Proverbs 1:15, the young man is advised not to expose himself to the path of evil by following sinners. It is to refuse to let someone take a certain path.
H4513.origine: The verb מָנַע comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of blocking, holding at a distance, creating a barrier. The original image is that of something being withheld, not allowed to pass. It is an active verb that implies a will to remove or to keep.
H4513.emploi: This verb appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs), and in the Psalms. In a strict sense, it expresses a direct refusal (Psalm 21:3), a physical blockage (Genesis 30:2), a retention of goods (Proverbs 11:26, Job 22:7). It is also used to describe God's action: He can prevent evil (1 Samuel 25:34), withhold His blessings (Amos 4:7), or deprive sinners of the fruits of their labor (Jeremiah 5:25). The verb often colors situations of injustice where someone refuses another what is due to them.
H4513.portee: This word invites the believer to honesty and generosity. Refusing the necessities to one who suffers, withholding good, preventing sharing — all of this is condemned by biblical wisdom and marked by a curse. Conversely, recognizing that only God can grant or refuse blessings helps to live with humility and gratitude. It is also a word of hope: when God does not refuse our legitimate requests, it is proof of His love.

sens: Metal or wooden rod that secures a door by sliding into brackets
Figuratively, that which closes or obstructs
H4514.detail:
1. A lock is a metal or wooden rod that is slid horizontally to secure a door from the inside or to block it. In the accounts of Nehemiah, the builders repairing the gates of Jerusalem installed locks as well as bars to secure them: "They covered it, and set up its doors, its locks, and its bars" (Nehemiah 3:3). The lock is one of the three essential parts of the ancient door, along with the doors (leaves) and the reinforcing bars.
2. Figuratively, the lock evokes what bars access or prevents opening. In the Song of Solomon, the young woman who rises to open to her beloved mentions "the handle of the lock" (Song of Solomon 5:5): the lock here symbolizes closure, the obstacle that must be removed for the encounter to take place.
H4514.origine: The Hebrew word מַנְעוּל (man'ul) comes from the root נעל (na'al), which means "to close" or "to lock." This root evokes the action of closing a door or access, and it appears in other words of the same family that designate closed doors or closing elements. The lock is therefore etymologically "that which closes" — the instrument of closure itself.
H4514.emploi: The word lock appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in two books. Five occurrences are found in the book of Nehemiah, in the detailed accounts of the repairs of the gates of Jerusalem upon the return from exile (chapters 3:3, 3:6, 3:13, 3:14, 3:15): each time a gate is restored, the text lists its three components: the doors, the locks, and the bars. These mentions emphasize the importance of the security of the rebuilt city. The sixth occurrence is found in the Song of Solomon (5:5), where the context is romantic and the lock takes on a symbolic nuance: it is no longer just a material mechanism, but an image of separation and closure of the heart.
H4514.portee: The lock in the biblical text reminds us that the security of the walls and gates of Jerusalem is essential to the life of the people, especially after the exile. It speaks to us of vigilance and protection. In the Song of Solomon, the lock invites us to reflect on what bars our access to love and what must be opened for the relationship to be true: an image of the heart that opens.

sens: Metal piece that secures and bars a door or gate
Closure of a shoe
Barrier, obstacle that maintains or defends
H4515.detail:
1. A lock is a metal element fixed to a door or gate to close and secure it — it is a simple closing system. In Deuteronomy 33:25, Moses blesses the tribe of Asher by promising that "your locks will be of iron and bronze": the image evokes solid and durable protection, comparable to fortress doors.
2. In the context of clothing and sandals, the lock can refer to the strap or clasp that holds a shoe in place, the closure that secures it to the foot.
3. Figuratively, the lock represents anything that bars, closes, or holds — an immaterial barrier that creates a limit or protection.
H4515.origine: The Hebrew word minʿal comes from a root meaning "to close" or "to retain." It is related to the idea of a bar or link that ensures cohesion and security. The same family of words expresses the action of putting on or securely closing something.
H4515.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:25, where it is found in the prophetic blessing of Moses addressed to the tribe of Asher. In this passage, "your locks will be of iron and bronze" is a promise of strength, stability, and divine protection. The military and geographical context — Asher was the tribe of the northern coast — reinforces the image of an unshakeable defense.
H4515.portee: This promise of locks of iron and bronze reminds believers that true security comes from God. It invites us to entrust to God the solidity and protection of our lives, knowing that His promises are as firm as the hardest metal.

sens: sought-after and abundant food served at a festive meal
by extension, refined and seductive pleasures
fig. anything that attracts and diverts from good
H4516.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a luxurious meal where one indulges in delicate and varied dishes — a banquet abundant with good things. It is the image of a generous table, suitable for celebrations and solemn occasions.
2. In a figurative sense, it evokes all the refined pleasures that seduce: the delights of body and spirit that capture attention. The psalmist prays: "Do not let my heart be drawn to what is evil, to take part in wicked deeds with men who are evil, and do not let me eat their delicacies!" (Psalms 141:4). Here, the feast of the wicked symbolizes not only their table but especially their entire way of life, their guilty pleasures, and their sinful habits.
3. From a spiritual perspective, the term can represent anything that diverts us from faithfulness to God: covetousness, sensual desires, or corrupting companionships.
H4516.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that essentially means "to be sweet, pleasant." It is a noun formed to designate what is tasty and pleasing to the palate — literally what "sweetens" and "enchants." The notion of pleasure is at the heart of the word, but the biblical context imbues this pleasure with moral significance: the innocent pleasure of good food coexists with the dangerous pleasure of temptation.
H4516.emploi: The word appears only once in Psalm 141:4, where it describes the feasts of men who do evil. In this context, it is not merely criticizing good food, but designating the entire realm of distractions and seductions that the sinner cultivates around them. The psalmist asks God to preserve his heart from these enticing traps, showing that the feast of the wicked is a symbol of a life of disobedience. This passage illustrates how Scripture does not condemn food itself, but the way it reflects a soul turned toward evil.
H4516.portee: This verse invites the believer to examine their heart: what are they being seduced by? To what "feasts" of wicked men are they participating? The word calls for vigilance against pleasures that isolate us from God and His will. It is a profound question about our true priorities: do we prefer the fleeting sweetness of sin, or communion with God?

sens: percussion musical instrument, consisting of a handle and a frame fitted with small metal rods or rings
object that produces a sound of crackling or rattling when shaken
H4517.detail:
1. The sistrum is a percussion musical instrument, formerly used in the Middle East and Egypt. It consists of a handle to which a frame, usually made of metal, is attached, equipped with small rods or rings that clatter and rattle when shaken. In 2 Samuel 6:5, David and all the Israelites play it during a solemn celebration before the Lord, alongside other musical instruments.
2. More broadly, the sistrum refers to any object used to produce sounds of crackling or vibration through the impact of its metal elements. It is an instrument that produces noise and joy, well-suited for religious celebrations and moments of rejoicing.
H4517.origine: The Hebrew word מְנַעֲנֵעַ (menan'a) comes from the root נָעַע (naa'), which means to shake, brandish, or agitate. This root evokes the physical and repeated action of moving something back and forth. The sistrum bears this name because its use consists precisely of shaking or agitating this instrument to produce a characteristic rattling sound.
H4517.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 6:5, during the account where King David dances and celebrates before the Lord with great joy. In this context, the sistrum is among the many musical instruments used to accompany this festive and religious procession. Its unique appearance suggests that it was a well-known and appreciated instrument in Israel for solemn and joyful occasions, although it is not mentioned as frequently as the harp or lyre.
H4517.portee: The sistrum reminds us that praise of God in the Bible is expressed through music, including that which makes noise and overflowing joy. This instrument shows us that God welcomes the noisy celebration and sincere rejoicing of His people, without demanding silent solemnity. It is an invitation to bodily, festive, and joyful praise, particularly visible in the dance and music that David offers before the ark of the Lord.

sens: cup or vessel intended for libations
utensil of the worship of the Tabernacle and the Temple
container holding a drink offering
H4518.detail: 1. The chalice is primarily a cup or a vessel of a particular shape, intended to pour or contain liquids (Exodus 25:29). 2. In the context of the Tabernacle and the Temple, it is a sacred utensil specifically used for libations, that is, liquid offerings poured out on the altar in accompaniment to sacrifices (Numbers 4:7). 3. These chalices were precious, generally made of pure gold for the utensils of the Tabernacle (Exodus 37:16), or of precious metals when belonging to the treasures of the Temple (Jeremiah 52:19).
H4518.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of purifying or pouring. It properly designates a serving vessel, particularly for worship. The form of the word indicates a utensil of precise function, which explains its constant use in the context of the objects of the Tabernacle and the Temple.
H4518.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in connection with worship service. Three occurrences describe the utensils of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25 and 37, Numbers 4), listing the chalices among the vessels intended to serve at the table in the sanctuary. One occurrence in Jeremiah 52:19 mentions the chalices among the treasures of the Temple plundered during the destruction of Jerusalem. The word thus exclusively designates these libation vessels, as distinct from other cups or basins of worship.
H4518.portee: These chalices remind the believer that every object of worship, even utilitarian, was consecrated and held sacred dignity. They symbolize the awareness that every act of worship, even the gestures of offering, was ordained by God for His people to honor Him with precision and respect. The fact that the chalices of the Temple could be broken or scattered illustrates the consequences of sin and God's judgment.

sens: Eldest son of Joseph, son of Israel, and founder of a tribe of Israel
The tribe descended from this son, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
The territory on the eastern side of the Jordan occupied by this tribe
Manasseh, king of Judah, son of King Hezekiah
Descendants of Manasseh who sent away their foreign wives during the time of Ezra
H4519G.detail:
1. Manasseh is the first son that Joseph had with Asenath in Egypt: Joseph named him this to signify that God had made him forget all his troubles and his father's house (Genesis 41:51). Manasseh receives the blessing from his father Israel, and his descendants become one of the most significant among the people of God.
2. The tribe of Manasseh descends from this son and is counted among the twelve tribes of Israel: it is regularly numbered in the censuses of the wilderness and plays an important role in the conquest of the land (Numbers 1:10; Numbers 26:28).
3. The tribe receives in inheritance the territory located east of the Jordan, along the river, as well as a portion west of the Jordan, making it a geographically extensive tribe (Joshua 13:29; 1 Chronicles 7:29).
4. Manasseh is also a king of Judah who reigned after his father Hezekiah, although this king is not mentioned in the references provided for the Hebrew word.
5. Some men named Manasseh lived during the time of the prophet Ezra and had to send away their foreign wives according to God's law.
H4519G.origine: The name Manasseh means "the one who makes forget" or "causing forgetfulness," formed from a root that expresses the action of forgetting or turning away memory. Joseph explicitly chose this name to commemorate God's mercy that allowed him to no longer remember his past sufferings: slavery, betrayal by his brothers, and separation from his family. This name thus evokes an act of divine grace, that of the erasure of pain.
H4519G.emploi: Manasseh first appears in Genesis as the newborn son of Joseph, then in the censuses of Numbers where the tribe is regularly counted among the warriors of Israel. Throughout the books of Joshua and Judges, the tribe of Manasseh occupies lands, receives Levitical cities, and participates in the wars of conquest of Canaan. In the time of Joshua, the sons of Manasseh do not fully conquer certain Canaanite cities (Joshua 17:12). The name also designates individuals during the time of Ezra who renounced their alliances with foreign women. The references attest to the use of the term more than a hundred times to designate the tribe, its territory, or its representatives.
H4519G.portee: The story of Manasseh teaches that God's forgiveness and mercy erase the wounds of the past: Joseph, who experienced injustice, abandonment, and slavery, receives renewal in Egypt and gives his son a name that proclaims divine grace. The tribe of Manasseh, despite its difficulties in conquering its inheritance, remains one of the strongest in Israel, showing that progressive obedience to God's plan bears fruit. For the believer, this name reminds us that God does not define us by our past sufferings, but by His ability to free us from them.

sens: King of Judah, son of Hezekiah and father of Amon
One who committed abominations and caused Judah to sin through idolatry
One whose actions led to the exile of Judah
H4519H.detail:
1. Manasseh is a king of Judah from the period of the divided monarchy. He is the son of King Hezekiah and succeeds his father on the throne (2 Kings 20:21). His son Amon will reign after him (2 Kings 21:18). He reigns for a long time over the kingdom and has much influence on the religious politics of the land.

2. Manasseh is distinguished by his actions contrary to the will of the Lord. He commits "abominations" by establishing idolatry on a large scale in Judah and leads the people to abandon the worship of the true God to serve other gods (2 Kings 21:11). His religious reforms are worse than those of the foreign peoples who once inhabited the land.

3. The biblical text states that Manasseh is "the direct cause of the exile": his sins and idolatry provoke the Lord's anger against Judah. Even after his death, the Lord does not relent in punishing the people for what he has done (2 Kings 23:26 and Jeremiah 15:4). His reign marks a catastrophic turning point for the kingdom.
H4519H.origine: The name Manasseh means "the one who makes forget" or "causing forgetfulness," from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of causing memory loss. This name first designated the eldest son of Joseph (progenitor of the tribe of Manasseh) in the Old Testament. The king who bears this same name in the 7th century BCE likely receives it to remind that God makes us forget our sufferings when He blesses us — a tragic irony in the case of this king who himself forgets the God of his fathers.
H4519H.emploi: Manasseh appears mainly in the books of Kings and Chronicles, where he is presented as one of the worst kings of Judah. He succeeds his father Hezekiah around 687 BCE and reigns for fifty-five years. The texts report his many sins: he restores the worship of idols, builds altars to false gods, sacrifices his own son, practices divination, and consecrates mediums (2 Kings 21:1-9). The Lord warns him through His prophets, but Manasseh and his people refuse to listen (2 Chronicles 33:10). The book of Chronicles adds a detail that Kings does not mention: after being captured by the Assyrians and imprisoned, Manasseh repents and the Lord restores him (2 Chronicles 33:11-13). However, the evil he has done in Judah persists and contributes to the final downfall of the kingdom. His name becomes synonymous with grave disobedience and sin that brings about divine judgment.
H4519H.portee: The story of Manasseh shows the power of one leader's sin to seduce an entire people and lead them away from God. It also teaches that even sincere repentance (related in 2 Chronicles) cannot erase the consequences of past actions on a nation. For the believer, the account of Manasseh serves as a warning: we must remain vigilant against modern idolatry and not allow leaders or culture to make us forget our covenant with God.

sens: son of Joseph and founder of a tribe of Israel
tribe descended from Manasseh, one of the twelve tribes of Israel
territory occupied by the tribe of Manasseh in the Promised Land
king of Judah, son of Hezekiah
man during the Exile who repudiated a foreign wife
H4519I.detail:
1. Manasseh is the firstborn son of Joseph and his Egyptian wife Asenath. He becomes the founder of one of the twelve tribes of Israel, alongside his brother Ephraim. His name means "the one who makes forget," which refers to Joseph's promise: God has made him forget his troubles.
2. The tribe of Manasseh is one of the great tribes of Israel, made up of all the descendants of Manasseh. It receives its own territory in the Promised Land, with its cities and borders.
3. The territory of Manasseh extends west of the Jordan, a fertile region important for the Northern Kingdom of Israel.
4. Manasseh is also the name of a king of Judah, son of King Hezekiah. He reigns for a long time over Judah but does evil in the eyes of the Lord, which leads to the Exile in Babylon.
5. At the time of the return from Exile, a man named Manasseh, a descendant of Pahath-Moab, is mentioned in Ezra 10:30 as having repudiated his foreign wife to obey the Law.
H4519I.origine: The name Manasseh means "the one who makes forget" in Hebrew, derived from the verb "to forget." Joseph gives this name to his firstborn son saying: "God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's household." It is a name that carries hope and divine comfort.
H4519I.emploi: Manasseh refers to several people and an important tribe in biblical history. The most famous is the firstborn son of Joseph, who becomes the leader of one of the twelve tribes and receives a territory in the Promised Land. Another Manasseh is a king of Judah, son of Hezekiah, who reigns for a long time but leads Judah into sin and Exile. A third Manasseh, mentioned only in Ezra 10:30, is a man from the time of the return from Exile who repudiates his foreign wife according to Ezra's decree. The name also appears to designate the tribe and territory of Manasseh in the Promised Land.
H4519I.portee: The name Manasseh reminds us that God grants relief and forgiveness: its very meaning, "the one who makes forget," expresses divine comfort. The story of King Manasseh, while showing the serious consequences of unfaithfulness, also manifests the possibility of repentance and return to God. Future generations can learn from his mistakes and reconnect with the Lord.

sens: Descendant of Pahath-moab who repudiated his foreign wife upon returning from exile
H4519J.detail: 1. Manasseh is one of the Israelites who, upon returning from exile in Babylon, had married a foreign woman and who, at the call of the prophet Ezra, agreed to repudiate her to conform to the law of Israel (Ezra 10:33). This act symbolized the renewal of the people's commitment to God after the catastrophe of exile.
H4519J.origine: The name Manasseh means in Hebrew "the one who makes forget" or "the one who causes forgetfulness." This same name was borne by the firstborn son of Joseph, founder of one of the major tribes of Israel, and by a king of Judah. Here, it designates an ordinary man from the return from exile, sharing the name of these great biblical figures.
H4519J.emploi: Manasseh appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:33, where he is listed among the descendants of Pahath-moab who repudiated their foreign wives. This passage is part of the account of the religious reform led by Ezra after the return from exile: the prophet urges the Israelites who returned from Babylon to separate from the non-Israelite women they had married during captivity, in order to preserve the religious and cultural purity of the people.

sens: Name given to Moses in a passage from Judges
The firstborn son of Joseph and founder of the tribe of Israel that bears his name
The tribe descended from Manasseh son of Joseph
The king of Judah son of Hezekiah
A man from the family of Pahath-Moab during the time of Ezra
A man from the family of Hashtum during the time of Ezra
H4519K.detail: 1. In Judges 18:30, "Manasseh" refers to Moses himself, called by this name in this unique passage — it is another name for the great legislator and prophet we generally know as Moses. 2. Manasseh is the firstborn son of Joseph and his Egyptian wife Asenath; he becomes the leader of a tribe of Israel that bears his name. 3. The tribe of Manasseh is one of the twelve peoples of Israel, with its inheritance lands in Canaan, first east of the Jordan, and then also west. 4. Manasseh son of Hezekiah became king of Judah after his father; he reigned for a long time and committed evil, leading to the exile of the kingdom. 5. Upon returning from exile, some men bearing this name — from the family of Pahath-Moab — had to send away their foreign wives. 6. Another Manasseh from the family of Hashtum experienced the same fate during the time of Ezra.
H4519K.origine: The name Manasseh means in Hebrew "the one who makes forget" or "causing forgetfulness." This meaning reflects the story of the first Manasseh: Joseph named him thus, saying that God made him forget his sufferings in Egypt. The name expresses how God erases the pain of the past through His goodness.
H4519K.emploi: Manasseh is a name borne by several people in the Bible. The provided passage, Judges 18:30, uses it as a second name for Moses in a genealogical note tracing back to Jonathan, grandson of Moses. But Manasseh primarily refers to the son of Joseph, whose tribe becomes one of the most powerful in Israel. It is also the name of a king of Judah known for his unfaithfulness to God, and that of ordinary men at the time of the return from exile.
H4519K.portee: Knowing the different figures bearing the name Manasseh shows how God works through generations: a name of hope — the forgetting of sufferings — accompanies men who experience various calls and failures. It is an invitation to see how God remains faithful despite our shortcomings.

sens: Member of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Joseph and grandson of Jacob
Inhabitant of the territories of Manasseh located east of the Jordan
Descendant of the people of Manasseh in later generations
H4520.detail:
1. The Manassites are the men and women who belong to the tribe of Manasseh, born of Joseph and Asenath. Manasseh himself, whose name means "to make forget," is the firstborn son of Joseph, and his tribe bears his name (Genesis 41:51).
2. The term particularly applies to the Manassites established east of the Jordan, in the regions of Gilead and Bashan. It is this half of the tribe that appears in the texts: they possess conquered lands and live on the eastern bank of the river (Deuteronomy 29:8).
3. By extension, the word designates all the descendants of this tribe through the generations, as seen during the wars of Israel or in the administrative organization of the kingdom (2 Kings 10:33).
H4520.origine: The word comes from מְנַשֶּׁה (Manasseh), which literally means "the one who makes forget" (root נשׁה, nacha). The name was given by Joseph to his firstborn son because God had comforted him and made him forget all his troubles (Genesis 41:51). The gentilice מְנַשִּׁי thus designates the members of this tribe, bearers of this family history.
H4520.emploi: The term "Manassites" appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in administrative or military lists. It always refers to the Manassites of Transjordan, never those of the west. In Deuteronomy, it appears alongside the Reubenites and Gadites, who share the same territory (Deuteronomy 4:43 and 29:8). In 2 Kings 10:33, the term encompasses the Manassites in the context of the Aramean wars against Israel. In 1 Chronicles 26:32, the Manassites appear again associated with other Transjordanian tribes in the organization of the affairs of the kingdom.
H4520.portee: Recognizing the Manassites is to see how God kept His promise to Joseph: his descendants multiplied and received an inheritance in the land of Israel, despite slavery and exile in Egypt. It is also to understand that Israel was never a simple unit, but a federation of twelve tribes, each with its territory, rights, and responsibilities before God. The people of God was built on this united diversity.

sens: part of a divided whole
allocation assigned to someone
what is allotted to someone as a share or inheritance
lot, destiny
H4521.detail:
1. A portion is primarily a material part, a piece or a quantity taken from a whole: in 2 Chronicles 31:3, the king gives a portion of his goods, meaning a share of his resources.

2. The word often refers to an official allocation, a regular share assigned by law or authority: in Nehemiah 12:44, the portions assigned by the law to the priests and Levites are guaranteed allocations, their right to sustenance.

3. A portion can be what belongs to someone in a division, an inheritance, or a fate: it is their share, what legally or morally belongs to them.

4. In a figurative sense, the portion becomes a destiny or fate, what is inevitably given to someone: in Psalms 11:6, the wicked have the cup of divine judgment as a bitter destiny that falls upon them.
H4521.origine: The Hebrew word מְנָת comes from a root that means "to count" and "to measure." A portion is literally "what is measured" or "what has been counted and assigned." This root evokes the idea of a fixed, delimited, definitive share. The related verb (מנה) appears in several biblical contexts related to determination and allocation.
H4521.emploi: The word appears eight times in the Old Testament, mostly in post-exilic narratives (Chronicles and Nehemiah) concerning the organization of worship and the sustenance of priests and Levites. In 2 Chronicles 31:3-4 and Nehemiah 12:44 and 12:47, it specifically designates the share of food or offerings legally due to the ministers of worship. In Nehemiah 13:10, the absence of delivered portions indicates a cultic crisis. Two passages broaden the meaning: in Psalms 11:6, it refers to the cup of divine judgment (what befalls the wicked), and in Jeremiah and Psalms 63:11, the coveted prey. Thus, the word is immersed in a context of legal order, established rights, and assigned destiny.
H4521.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Bible cares about concrete justice: everyone should receive their portion, their legitimate share. For the ministers of worship, it is a promise that the Lord watches over their sustenance. For sinners, it is a warning: divine judgment is an inevitable and measured portion. The word invites both justice towards others and trust in divine providence.

sens: group of forced workers or slaves
mandatory work, forced service without pay
burden, load imposed on someone
tax or tribute payable in labor or money
one who is subject to this obligation
agent responsible for collecting or organizing this obligation
H4522.detail:
1. The word first designates a group of men requisitioned for mandatory work: in Egypt, Pharaoh organizes "corvées" for construction (Exodus 1:11); Solomon uses corvées to build the Temple and his palaces (1 Kings 5:14).
2. By extension, it refers to the forced labor itself, unpaid: Genesis 49:15 speaks of a man who "submits to a tribute," meaning he accepts an obligation of work or payment.
3. The word also evokes the burden or load that this represents: to bear a corvée is to be bent under the weight.
4. It then designates the tax or tribute, often demanded by a king victorious over conquered peoples: the defeated Canaanites "were subjected to a tribute" (Joshua 16:10).
5. The word can also refer to the person who undergoes this obligation: a "tributary" or a subject.
6. Finally, it names the official responsible for collecting these taxes or organizing these corvées: Adoram is "overseer of the tribute" (2 Samuel 20:24).
H4522.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to pull, to take away, to remove." The image is that of a burden that is taken away or imposed: something is taken from someone (their work, their money, their freedom). Words from the same family express the idea of obligation, constraint, subtraction.
H4522.emploi: The word appears 22 times, mainly in historical books (Kings, Chronicles, Joshua, Judges) and occasionally in poetic ones (Proverbs, Lamentations). It is primarily used to describe: (1) the corvées imposed by political powers, notably the kings of Israel (especially Solomon) and the pharaohs of Egypt; (2) the tributes imposed on conquered or subjected peoples; (3) royal taxes; (4) the officials of these systems. The context is often one of servitude and oppression: those who undergo a corvée lose their freedom and their property.
H4522.portee: This word reminds the reader that the enslavement and exploitation of human labor are a reality of sin. It also exposes how the kings of Israel, notably Solomon, replicated the injustices of Egypt by imposing corvées on their own people. For the Christian, it is a call to recognize the dignity of work, the respect owed to each person, and the rejection of any system that reduces man to slavery.

sens: The feeling of pity towards one who suffers
Tenderness and gentleness towards the unfortunate
H4523.detail:
1. This word designates the feeling of tenderness and pity one experiences in the face of another's suffering. It is the heart that is moved by distress. In Job 6:14, the friend of the suffering just "has a right to compassion": this means that in the face of one who is overwhelmed, even if their faith falters, one can only empathize with gentleness.
2. Compassion is this active tenderness that drives one to support the unfortunate. It stands in opposition to hardness or indifference. It is what is sorely lacking when one abandons the one who weeps.
H4523.origine: The Hebrew word mas comes from a root that evokes the bending, the yielding of one who collapses under weight. Compassion is thus this inclination of the heart towards one who is crumbling: one bends with them, one leans over their misery. That is why it is the attitude contrary to the hardness of those who judge without mercy.
H4523.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 6:14. The context is poignant: Job, overwhelmed by his misfortunes and the misunderstanding of his friends, reminds his companions that a friend must show compassion towards one who suffers. This passage reveals how the Bible understands friendship: not as a matter of judgment or condemnation, but as shared tenderness in the face of suffering.
H4523.portee: This word challenges our way of treating those who suffer. We are called to develop true compassion: not a superficial pity, but this inclination of the heart that drives us to weep with those who weep and to support them without judgment. It is the evangelical call to bear one another's burdens.

sens: The set of what surrounds, what encircles a place or a person
Surroundings, neighboring area of a city or territory
What revolves around, what gravitates, movement or circulation around a central point
Immediate entourage of a person
H4524.detail:
1. The word fundamentally designates what surrounds something or someone — the space, the places, the beings that gravitate around. In Jerusalem, the priests of the idols roamed not only the city itself but also its "surroundings" (2 Kings 23:5), the villages and countryside that encircled it.
2. "Surroundings" also indicates the neighboring region of a place, its vicinity. It is the area that extends around a center, accessible and linked to that center.
3. The word can evoke a circular movement or an evolution around an axis. The clouds, in their "evolution" (Job 37:12), turn and unfold according to God's orders — the image is that of elements in orbital motion around a point.
4. When speaking of people, it refers to the immediate entourage, those who are very close, who surround. The enemies who "surround" the righteous (Psalms 140:10) press him on all sides, encircling him in their hostility.
H4524.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to turn," "to go around." This image of rotation, of what returns around a center, naturally extends to "what surrounds," "what encircles." The same root gives rise to words related to circular movement and the surroundings of a place. The basic idea is geometric: a circle, a circumference.
H4524.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the nuance of a sphere or an area that encompasses. In 2 Kings 23:5, it designates the geographical surroundings of Jerusalem. In Job 37:12, it depicts the evolutions of the clouds, their circular dance. In Psalms 140:10, it evokes the hostility that surrounds the psalmist on all sides. In Song of Solomon 1:12, the "entourage" of the king is the immediate context where the lover is found. Each time, the idea of a circle, of what envelops or encircles, is present.
H4524.portee: This word reminds us that we always live in a context, surrounded by realities that affect us — places, people, influences. For the Christian, this invites awareness of their "spiritual environment," the forces and presences that surround them, and to ask God for wisdom to navigate this context with discernment and faithfulness.

sens: One who manufactures or repairs locks and metal fittings
One who locks up or guards a prisoner
Prison, place of detention
Fortified enclosure or closed construction
H4525.detail:
1. The locksmith is a metal craftsman: he manufactures locks, bolts, chains, and all the fittings that close and secure. It is a recognized and specialized trade. We see it in 2 Kings 24:14, where Nebuchadnezzar takes captive "all the craftsmen and the locksmiths": the Babylonian king wants to appropriate these skilled men because their military and technical talents make him powerful.
2. By extension, the locksmith becomes one who locks up, who keeps someone behind a closed door. He is a jailer, a prison guard.
3. The prison itself, the cell where captives are held. Psalms 142:8 cries out: "Bring my soul out of prison," expressing the confinement and distress of the captive. Isaiah 42:7 speaks of "bringing out the captive from prison."
4. More broadly, any closed and fortified construction: the bulwarks, enclosures, ramparts that enclose or protect a city.
H4525.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to close," "to lock up," "to shut." The root is also visible in other Hebrew words related to enclosure and confinement. The starting image is that of a door closing, a lock securing: the one who masters this mechanism is the locksmith, and the place where one is locked up is the prison. This is why the same word designates the craftsman, the action of locking up, and the place of confinement.
H4525.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Old Testament. In 2 Kings 24:14 and 24:16, it specifically designates the locksmiths that Nebuchadnezzar deports to Babylon: these are skilled men, specialists alongside the carpenters, taken to serve the conquering king. In the Psalms and Isaiah (Psalms 142:8, Isaiah 24:22 and 42:7), the word changes meaning and designates the prison or cell: the place where captives and prisoners are locked up. Jeremiah 24:1 returns to the meaning of "locksmith" in the context of the Babylonian deportation. The context determines which of the two meanings is intended: the craftsman when speaking of deported men, the prison when discussing confinement and liberation.
H4525.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of two truths. First, that there are diverse talents — the locksmith, the carpenter — and that God is glorified through every faithful trade. Secondly, and more profoundly, the word "prison" resonates with the biblical theme of spiritual captivity and deliverance: Isaiah 42:7 announces the Messiah who frees the captives from darkness, an image of salvation in Jesus Christ who breaks the chains of sin and death.

sens: Flat surface that is part of a structure or piece of furniture
Edge or border that frames or protects a surface
Fortified outwork serving for defense
H4526.detail:
1. The panel is a flat surface that constitutes an element of a larger structure. This is clearly seen in the furniture of the temple: the panels of the sacred chariots, located between the uprights, were engraved with motifs (lions, oxen, cherubim) and formed the visible faces of the furniture (1 Kings 7:29).
2. The edge or border is the part that frames and protects: on the gold table of the sanctuary, a border four fingers high ran all around to prevent objects from falling, and a gold border was placed on it for ornamentation (Exodus 25:25). It is the "belt" that frames.
3. The fortified outwork is a fortress or defended refuge: this is the figurative use of the word, as when one speaks of trembling "out of their fortresses" (2 Samuel 22:46), that is, away from their strong points, their military refuges. The image comes from the closed surface that surrounds and protects.
H4526.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to close" or "to surround." The term panel first evokes the idea of what is closed, surrounded, limited by edges. The word appears mainly to describe architectural elements or temple furniture, where the notion of a flat surface that surrounds or delineates is very concrete.
H4526.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Bible, mostly in the description of the furniture and structures of the temple. In Exodus, it designates the edge of the gold table (Exodus 25:25, 37:12). In 1 Kings, it mainly refers to the panels of the sacred chariots made by Hiram (1 Kings 7:28-36), which were the decorated, visible flat surfaces bearing engravings. In 2 Samuel, Psalms, and Micah, the word takes on a figurative sense to describe the "fortresses" or fortified refuges, the strong places where one retreats. It is the same notion of enclosure and protection, applied to military defense.
H4526.portee: This word reminds us of the meticulous attention that God required for the furniture of His sanctuary: every detail, every panel, every edge was ordered according to a precise plan. It invites the believer to see that God reigns even over the small things, and that His order extends to all elements of worship. Spiritually, it also speaks to us of refuge and protection: where we find our true fortresses, our true security.

sens: solid base on which a construction is built
essential element that supports the whole
what lays the first layer of a structure
H4527.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the foundation is the stone base on which a building is constructed. In the passage from 1 Kings 7:9, it refers to the magnificent cut stones that form the foundations of the temple and the constructions of Solomon — the deepest base, from which one builds up to the highest cornices.
2. By extension, the foundation refers to anything that lays the first layer, the primary and indispensable element that allows the whole to stand and endure.
H4527.origine: The Hebrew word masad comes from a root that evokes the idea of fixing, establishing solidly. It is close to the notion of "base" or "foundation" — what is laid first, what supports everything else. The word belongs to the family of construction and building terms, fundamental in the architectural language of the Bible.
H4527.emploi: The word masad appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 7:9. It describes the foundation stones of the temple in Jerusalem and the palaces built by Solomon. These stones, beautifully cut and fitted, form the solid base — the foundation — that extends from the depths to the high parts of the edifice. The unique usage in a context of royal architecture underscores the importance of a solid foundation for great constructions.
H4527.portee: For the Christian reader, the foundation reminds us that every lasting edifice rests on a solid base. Spiritually, this evokes the importance of a firm foundation — whether moral, spiritual, or doctrinal — on which to build one's life and faith. Without a solid foundation, no structure can stand.

sens: Covered gallery bordered by columns at the entrance of a building
Transitional space between the outside and the inside of a house
Figure of protection or passage
H4528.detail:
1. A portico is a covered gallery or passage, supported by columns or pillars, that extends in front of the entrance of a building — here the upper chamber of Eglon. It is an architectural space that offers both protection and transition between the outside and the inside.
2. In the context of the account in Judges 3:23, the portico is the place through which Ehud escapes after killing King Eglon: he passes through it and closes the doors of the chamber behind him, creating a barrier between him and his pursuers. The word thus designates a passage or corridor here.
3. On a spiritual level, a portico can evoke a threshold, a place of passage or transition — here from God's judgment (the assassination of the tyrant) to the deliverance of the people.
H4528.origine: The Hebrew word מִסְדְּרוֹן (misderôn) is built on a root that suggests order or arrangement (סדר, sedar). A portico is indeed an "arranged" or "organized" space, a succession of columns in a regular order. The presence of this unique word in the Bible makes its precise meaning difficult to establish, but the architectural and historical context — royal palaces in the Levant all had porticos — clearly indicates an element of entry or passage.
H4528.emploi: The word appears only once in Judges 3:23, during the murder of King Eglon by Ehud. The context shows that it is a transitional space: Ehud passes through it to escape, then closes the doors behind him. This unique passage testifies to the architectural reality of royal residences in the ancient Levant, where the portico was a common and recognizable element for biblical readers.
H4528.portee: This word reminds us that even the concrete details of biblical narratives — here the architecture of a house — participate in the unfolding of divine action and deliverance. The portico, an apparently mundane detail, is the path by which Ehud escapes the oppressive king and becomes the instrument of Israel's freedom.

sens: To transform into liquid, to lose solidity
