4. What remains hidden, buried, invisible: in Isaiah 45:3, God promises "hidden treasures, buried riches." It is also what is concealed from view, like the tears shed "in secret" in Jeremiah 13:17.
H4565.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root סתר (s.t.r.) which means "to hide," "to cover." The same verb regularly appears in the Old Testament in the sense of "to hide" or "to conceal." The noun מִסְתָּר retains this idea of what is covered, withdrawn, protected from sight — either for safety or to act without witnesses.
H4565.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and the prophets. It primarily designates the refuge or den from which the wicked spies on his prey (Psalms 10, 17) — an image of the lurking predator. It also applies to the place where one commits crime in secret (Psalms 64), away from all sight. More broadly, it qualifies what is hidden and concealed, like treasures or buried riches (Isaiah 45:3). The word can also describe what is done or suffered out of sight: the tears shed "in secret" (Jeremiah 13:17) for the shame of Israel.
H4565.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees everything, even what is done in secret. The psalmist paints the wicked who believes he can escape notice by acting from his secret lair — but God "knows everything" (Jeremiah 23:24). It is a call to conscience: no crime escapes the Lord. Conversely, it is also a comfort: when faith retreats "in secret" to weep or pray, God witnesses it and does not abandon it.

sens: Action of one who works, completed work
Visible result of work, production
Moral act or action, virtue or vice
H4566.detail:
1. The work refers to the labor one does, the fruit of effort and toil. In Job 34:25, the word speaks of the works of the wicked that God knows perfectly — what they do, how they act in darkness: it is their conduct, their activity.
2. The word can also refer to what is produced, created, constructed by work — the finished work that one looks at and appreciates.
3. In a moral and spiritual sense, a "work" is an action that reveals the heart and intentions: a good or bad work testifies to the character of the one who performs it.
H4566.origine: The Aramaic word מַעְבָּד (ma'bad) comes from a root meaning "to work, to make." It is a form of noun that expresses the idea of work and production. Hebrew uses related roots to express work and labor. The Aramaic word is akin to other Semitic terms that denote action, task, and labor.
H4566.emploi: This word appears only once in the French Bible, in Job 34:25. It is used in Elihu's speech to Job to affirm that God sees and knows the works of all men, even those committed in darkness. The context is one of affirming divine justice: God watches the acts of each person and renders justice according to actions. The word emphasizes that nothing escapes God's gaze, even hidden works.
H4566.portee: This word reminds us that God sees all our actions, good or bad, even those we hide. It invites the Christian to live with the awareness that their entire life is before God, and that it is through our works that our faith is manifested and that God judges our hearts.

sens: Action, completed work
Act, manifestation of a power
Production, result of a work
H4567.detail:
1. The word primarily designates an action, a work that one executes or has completed. It is the concrete result of effort and skill.
2. It can also evoke the action of a higher power — here, in Daniel 4:37, the "works" of the king of heaven are his acts in history, all that he accomplishes and manifests through his authority. It is the visible trace of his sovereignty.
3. More broadly, it is what one produces, what one creates: a work is something durable, bearing the mark of its maker.
H4567.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of doing, working, producing. It is related to words that designate work, task, accomplishment. It is a solid and common term for naming what is made or realized — whether it is a simple task or divine action.
H4567.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:37, in the confession of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar. There, it is used to designate the actions of the King of heaven — his works are "true" and his ways "just." It is a term that values what is done, affirming that each act, each result, reflects the nature and will of the one who acts.
H4567.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God is not absent or silent: his actions in history are real, reliable, and just. The "works" of God do not deceive — they reveal who he is. It is an encouragement to recognize God's hand in what he accomplishes and to trust him.

sens: characteristic of what is thick, having a large dimension from one side to the other
H4568.detail: 1. The word concretely designates the thickness of an object — the dimension that separates its two faces. In 1 Kings 7:46, it refers to the thickness of the massive bronze vessels that Hiram makes for the temple: the text specifies that these containers are cast in the earth, which requires a certain mass and density of material to be solid and durable.
H4568.origine: The word comes from the root עבה ("to be thick, to become heavy"). It conveys the idea of a dense and compact material, that of an object that takes up space, that has weight and substance. It is a concrete, material term, without notable figurative extension.
H4568.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 7:46, in the passage where the narrator describes the bronze casting works commissioned by King Solomon to adorn the temple. It is a technical, precise term to designate a measurable physical dimension, one of the three dimensions of matter.

sens: Shallow crossing of a watercourse, a shallow place where one can cross
Strategic position, narrow passage or defile
Blow, strike of a rod hitting
H4569A.detail:
1. A ford is a place in a watercourse where the water is shallow: one can cross it on foot without danger. It is a natural crossing that travelers and herds seek to cross rivers. In Genesis 32:22, Jacob "crossed the ford of Jabbok" with all his family and possessions: the ford is the only way to cross this river that formed a boundary between the lands.
2. The word also refers to a strategic crossing on land: a position where traffic is concentrated and can be controlled or defended. In 1 Samuel 13:23, "A garrison of Philistines took up position at the pass of Micmash": this is a narrow place through which troops can only pass with difficulty, and which the enemy can monitor or block.
3. By extension of the meaning of "blow" or "striking blow", the word refers to the action itself: in Isaiah 30:32, "At every blow of the rod that is destined for him", it is each strike, each passage of the rod on the back of the guilty one.
H4569A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to pass" or "to cross over". It is built on the root that describes the action of overcoming an obstacle, passing from one side to the other. The ford is therefore literally "the place of passage" or "that by which one passes" — the point where crossing becomes possible. It is a common word in the description of travels and movements in the land of Israel, where rivers constituted major obstacles.
H4569A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible with three nuances. First, it very concretely designates a ford: the ford of Jabbok, a major boundary of Canaan (Genesis 32:22). Next, it qualifies a strategic land passage, a defile that the Philistines occupy militarily (1 Samuel 13:23): the image remains that of a narrow and controllable place. Finally, it takes on the figurative meaning of "blow" or "striking blow" (Isaiah 30:32), where the action of striking is seen as a succession of passages, blows that fall. The three uses retain the idea of a passage or an action that crosses.
H4569A.portee: The ford reminds the reader that on the journey of faith, there are necessary crossings, places where one must dare to pass. Jacob at the ford of Jabbok encounters God there (the day after his crossing). The notion of a strategic crossing and a guarded ford invites recognition that God controls the passages of our lives — nothing opposes His will, and every obstacle has meaning in His plan.

sens: Point where a river can be crossed on foot or with a vehicle
Narrow passage or defile in mountainous or steep terrain
Action of crossing a watercourse or a difficult passage
H4569B.detail:
1. A ford is a shallow place in a river where one can cross without a boat. It is a natural and regularly used crossing. In Joshua 2:7, the spies are pursued towards the "ford" of the Jordan: it is the usual place where the river is crossed. In Judges 3:28 and 12:5-6, the fords of the Jordan are strategic control points: whoever masters access commands who can flee or advance.

2. The word also refers to a narrow passage in the mountains, a defile. In 1 Samuel 14:4, Jonathan seeks to reach the enemy post "between the passes": these are narrow points in the terrain. In Isaiah 10:29, "they pass the defile" describes invaders crossing a mountain pass.

3. By extension, it means the very action of crossing, the passage. The word evokes the idea of overcoming an obstacle: a river, a mountain, a line of defense.
H4569B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to pass" or "to cross over". It is also the basis of "Hebrew" (ivri), the one who has "crossed" the Euphrates River according to tradition. The image is that of movement overcoming a natural obstacle: the ford is the point where one can pass. It is an action noun that has become a place name.
H4569B.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives. In Judges 3 and 12, the fords are places of military control and confrontation: Ehud and his men intercept the Moabites there, Gilead filters the fugitives from Ephraim. In Joshua 2, the ford of the Jordan is the natural escape route after the spying of Jericho. In Isaiah 10 and 16, Jeremiah 51, the passages and defiles serve to describe the routes of invasion or flight of enemies. The word thus moves from the geographical (a physical place) to the strategic (a control point) to the poetic (the route of calamity).
H4569B.portee: The ford reminds us that in spiritual life, some crossings are decisive. It is at these crucial points that battles are fought, where faith is tested, and where God's enemies are stopped. For the Christian, this invites recognition of the moments when God controls the "passages" of their life and determines who can advance and who is stopped.

sens: Physical path, track, or road taken
Set of tents and installations where soldiers camp
Line of behavior or conduct, moral or spiritual
H4570.detail:
1. The path is primarily a way taken for movement: it is the track marked on the ground, the road followed on foot. In 1 Samuel 17:20, David takes a path to join the army in battle.
2. By extension, the word designates the military camp itself, the organized set of tents and positions where soldiers camp. In 1 Samuel 26:7, it is in the heart of the sleeping camp that David and Abishai approach Saul.
3. Figuratively, the path becomes the way of life, the moral or spiritual line of conduct followed: the itinerary of our actions and choices. In Psalms 23:3, God "leads me in paths of righteousness" — it is the road of uprightness. In Proverbs 2:15 and 4:11, "crooked paths" are contrasted with "paths of righteousness": each person follows a moral path that belongs to them.
H4570.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to turn, to go around", hence the initial image of circumvallation, the trench that goes around a besieged stronghold. From there, it came to designate first the fortified camp, then more broadly any path or road — anything that is "drawn" and "traced". The root evokes circular movement, the mark left by repeated steps.
H4570.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in biblical poetry (Psalms, Proverbs) and in historical narratives. In military context, it describes the camp, the temporary installation of soldiers (1 Samuel 17:20, 26:7). But the most common and richest meaning is that of the way of life: the Psalms and Proverbs use it to speak of the moral and spiritual paths that God invites us to follow, or conversely the misguided paths that the wicked take. The context varies: sometimes "the path" is straight, narrow, and just; sometimes it is crooked, winding, leading to destruction. The image remains that of a visible, marked trajectory that can be followed or forsaken.
H4570.portee: This word invites the believer to see their life as a walk on a path: God does not abandon those who seek Him, He "leads them in paths of righteousness". Each day, we take a moral path; faith is recognizing that God guides us, while refusing His direction leads to wandering on the crooked paths of the wicked. The word helps to live faith as a conscious journey, where each step counts.

sens: To lose balance, to physically waver
To be unstable, uncertain in one's walk or position
To weaken morally or spiritually, to lack firmness
To be shaken or disturbed by an external force
H4571.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to waver on one's legs, to risk falling. It is the image of a foot slipping or a body that can no longer stand firmly. In 2 Samuel 22:37, the psalmist says that his feet do not stumble: he walks confidently on the path that God has widened for him.

2. The word also evokes general instability, a lack of firmness in position or walk. One who stumbles is poorly assured, wavering. In Job 12:5, the one whose foot stumbles becomes an object of contempt: he is a stumbling man, unreliable.

3. Transposed to the moral and spiritual domain, to stumble means to weaken in one's trust, integrity, or faith. In Psalms 26:1, the psalmist asserts that he walks in integrity and does not stumble: he remains firm in his commitment to the Lord. Similarly, in Psalms 37:31, the one whose law of God is in his heart sees his steps not stumble.

4. The word can also express the action of being shaken or disturbed by a force: to make someone stumble means to shake them. In Psalms 69:24, the psalmist asks God to continually make the loins of his enemies stumble, that is, to shake them, to disturb them.
H4571.origine: The Hebrew verb מָעַד (ma'ad) belongs to a family of words evoking slipping and instability. The root expresses the idea of losing grip, of not holding firmly. It is the origin of the noun that designates one who trips or slips. The verb can be used in the simple voice (Qal) to describe someone who stumbles by themselves, or in the causative voice (Hiphil) to express the action of making someone stumble, of shaking them.
H4571.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the Psalms, 2 Samuel, and Job. It is primarily used in the negative: "my feet do not stumble" (2 Samuel 22:37, Psalms 18:37, Psalms 26:1, Psalms 37:31). This negation affirms the stability of the righteous, their unshakeability in the face of trials. In contrast, Job 12:5 describes the one whose foot stumbles as being in misfortune and exposed to contempt. In Psalms 69:24, the verb in the causative voice expresses the action of shaking the enemies. The word thus remains concentrated in contexts where spiritual stability or the firmness of the righteous in the face of adversity is at stake.
H4571.portee: This word reveals the biblical faith in the stability of the righteous. For the believer, not stumbling means remaining firm in integrity despite difficulties, relying on trust in God. To stumble, on the contrary, is to allow oneself to be shaken by doubt or fear. By reading this word, we discover that spiritual stability is not natural: it is a gift from God to the believer who trusts Him and meditates on His law. It is an invitation to ask God to strengthen us on the path He opens before us.

sens: Man mentioned during the return from exile under Ezra
H4572.detail: Maadaï is a man from the tribe of Bani, living at the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:34, among those who agreed to put away the foreign wives they had married, in accordance with Ezra's instructions to restore the religious purity of the people returning to Jerusalem.
H4572.origine: The name Maadaï literally means "ornament of Jehovah" or "adornment of the Lord." It is composed of מַע (ma, which evokes appearance or ornament) and יָהּ (Yah, a contracted form of the divine name). It is a typical name among the Hebrews, who expressed their piety and belonging to God through their proper names.
H4572.emploi: Maadaï appears only once in the Scriptures, in Ezra 10:34. He is mentioned in the list of men from the sons of Bani who put away their foreign wives during the return from exile. This passage shows that Maadaï joined the reform movement initiated by Ezra to preserve the religious identity of Israel by separating from mixed marriages. His inclusion in this list honors his participation in this decisive moment in the history of the people.

sens: Priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H4573.detail: Maadia is a priest who participated in the return from exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:5). His name appears in the list of priests and Levites who came up from Babylon to rebuild the temple and the community in Jerusalem after the captivity.
H4573.origine: The Hebrew name Maadia literally means "adorned by JAH" or "decorated by God." It is composed of "ma'" (to adorn, to embellish) and "Jah" (abbreviation of the divine name). This name expresses the idea that its bearer is marked by the grace and beauty of God. It is also known in the variants Moadiah (Nehemiah 12:17) and Maaziah (Nehemiah 10:8), all priests from the same family or close generations.
H4573.emploi: Maadia is mentioned only once in the Segond (Nehemiah 12:5) as one of the priests who returned from captivity in Babylon with Zerubbabel. His name appears in the official list of religious leaders responsible for restoring temple worship. Variants of his name appear elsewhere (Moadiah in Nehemiah 12:17, Maaziah in Nehemiah 10:8), showing that his family held an important place among the restored clergy.
H4573.portee: This name reminds us that God does not allow His people to be forgotten in exile: even in the midst of captivity, men like Maadia maintain their faith and return to rebuild worship. His name, "adorned by God," encourages the believer to remember that God adorns with His grace those who remain faithful to Him.

sens: Refined and succulent food, exquisite flavor
Pleasure, enjoyment, delight
Object of desire or personal satisfaction
H4574.detail:
1. The word primarily designates fine and delicate food that pleases the palate: Asher "will provide the delicacies of kings" (Genesis 49:20), an image of the abundance and quality of the products that his land will produce. It is the food of princes, not that of ordinary people.
2. By extension, the word takes on the meaning of "delight" or "pleasure": a well-educated child "will bring delight to [the soul]" of his father (Proverbs 29:17), a moral and emotional satisfaction, not just gustatory.
3. The contrast in Lamentations 4:5 — those "nourished with delicacies" who "perish in the streets" — shows that this word also designates the state of wealth and enjoyment: the loss of these delights symbolizes total collapse, the transition from prosperity to misery.
H4574.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of sweetness and pleasantness. It belongs to the family of words designating delectation, the pleasure of the senses. The biblical context associates it with material wealth and earthly well-being, which often places it in tension with calls for sobriety and justice.
H4574.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used in contexts of prosperity (blessing of the tribe of Asher), moral education (the child who pleases the father), and in the laments over the fall of Jerusalem. Its usage reveals an ambivalence: the "delicacies" are both a sign of divine blessing and a risk of attachment to earthly goods. Refined food characterizes the powerful and the rich, but also those who run the risk of losing everything.
H4574.portee: This word reminds us that material blessings — food, well-being, legitimate pleasures — are a gift from God and a source of gratitude. However, excessive attachment to earthly delights can blind us to true values: Lamentations shows that those who live only for these pleasures collapse when they disappear. The Christian can receive the delights of life with gratitude, but without placing their heart in them.

sens: Cord, cable, or knot that attaches, unites
Set of links that hold something together
State of being bound, chained
H4575.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a material link: a rope, a cable, a knot that holds or attaches. In Job 38:31, God speaks of the "links of the Pleiades" — the invisible links that hold together the stars of this constellation, creating a cosmic unity.
2. By extension, it can evoke the set of links that form a chain or a system (think of a fishing net where the knots are interconnected). It conveys the idea of what holds multiple things together in a structured way.
3. Figuratively and rarely, the word can also suggest the idea of servitude or subjugation — the state of one who is held captive, although this meaning is not developed in our usages.
H4575.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "tying," "binding," or "loosing." The feminine plural form (with the suffix -ôt) often suggests several links or a set of interwoven links. It is the concrete vocabulary of manual labor and craftsmanship: one who weaves, ties ropes, creates attachments.
H4575.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 15:32, Agag approaches "joyfully" — here an ancient translation likely interpreted the word in a fixed manner, perhaps as an expression of attitude or haughty bearing. But the main and certain usage is Job 38:31, where God questions Job about his ability to bind or loose the links of the stellar constellations. It is a passage of pure cosmic wonder: the links that maintain the order of the heavens and the cohesion of the visible universe.
H4575.portee: This word reminds us that everything in creation — even the stars in the sky — is linked, organized, maintained by a creative intention. For the believer, it is an invitation to contemplate the invisible order that supports the visible world and to recognize the Creator behind this harmony. It is also a call to humility: only God masters these cosmic links.

sens: agricultural tool with a flat blade for turning the soil
by extension, any action of cultivating or working the land
H4576.detail:
1. The spade is an agricultural tool, equipped with a wide, flat blade, used for turning, digging, and preparing the soil before sowing. In Isaiah 7:25, it specifically refers to the instrument with which men cultivated the fertile mountains of Judah: it is manual, concrete work that requires effort and sweat.
2. By extension, the word can evoke the work of the land itself, the activity of cultivation and soil preparation. In the prophetic context of Isaiah, the mountains once tilled with the spade will be abandoned to thorns and briars — a sign of ruin, a return to a wild state.
H4576.origine: The Hebrew word ma'ader comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to hoe." It belongs to the family of cutting tools and actions of cutting or tearing. In Greek, this word is rendered by σκαπάνη (skapanê), the same term used to denote a spade or shovel. The agricultural context and practical usage of the term clearly situate it within the vocabulary of rural life in ancient Israel.
H4576.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew biblical text, in Isaiah 7:25. The Segond translates it as "spade." This prophetic passage speaks of the judgment that will strike the land of Judah: the lands once carefully cultivated with the spade will become barren and wild, overrun by thorns. It is a sign of desolation and divine punishment — the contrast between the order of human labor and the chaos of abandoned nature.
H4576.portee: This word reminds us of the creation order where man must cultivate the land through work and effort. Its appearance in a judgment oracle emphasizes that the abandonment of the land, the return to wildness, is a consequence of sin and unfaithfulness. It is an invitation to see agricultural labor not as a curse, but as an effect of divine grace that allows man to dwell and be nourished on the earth. When this work ceases, it is a sign of a rupture between God and His people.

sens: The part of the body between the chest and the hips, the abdomen
Figuratively, the seat of desires and appetites
H4577.detail: 1. The belly is the region of the body that extends from the chest to the hips. It is where the essential internal organs for life (stomach, intestines) are located. In Daniel 2:32, the statue in Nebuchadnezzar's dream has a belly and thighs of bronze, a distinct part of the body from the chest (silver) and the head (gold). 2. In the Bible generally, the belly often symbolizes carnal desires or appetite: what drives us to satisfy our most immediate needs, far from what is spiritual.
H4577.origine: This Aramaic word (méʿah) comes from the same root as the Hebrew méʿeh (belly, H4578), both simply designating the cavity of the body where vital organs reside. The family of this word in Hebrew describes the seat of emotions and appetites — a common image in the Old Testament, where the belly symbolizes instincts and desires.
H4577.emploi: This word appears only once in Daniel 2:32, in the account of Nebuchadnezzar's dream. The statue that the prophet sees has several parts: the head of gold represents Babylon, and the belly of bronze (as well as the thighs) symbolizes a future empire. The usage here is purely descriptive and anatomical, situating a part of the body within an allegorical composition.
H4577.portee: This mention of the belly in Nebuchadnezzar's vision reminds us that our entire body — including our appetites and desires — is known to God and is part of His plan for history. It invites the believer not to be enslaved by his belly (Philippians 3:19), but to master his carnal appetites in order to follow God.

sens: The interior of the body, particularly the belly and digestive organs
The organ of procreation, the womb
The offspring, the children born from the body
The seat of emotions: compassion, love, anguish, pain
H4578.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the internal organs of the human body, especially the belly and everything it contains. It is a concrete and physical term: in Psalms 71:6, the psalmist speaks of the "belly of my mother" to evoke the time before his birth. 2. It can specifically refer to the womb, the maternal organ from which children are born. In 2 Samuel 7:12, it speaks of one who "will come from your entrails," meaning the son that a woman will carry within her. 3. By natural extension, the word moves from the organ to the fruit of that organ: it signifies children, descendants. In Genesis 15:4, the Lord promises Abram that "one who will come from your entrails will be your heir" — He is speaking of a son to be born. 4. Finally, and especially in poetic texts, the entrails become the emotional seat: they express the movements of the heart. In Lamentations 2:11, the prophet says that his "entrails are boiling" to describe his anguish in the face of disaster. In Isaiah 63:15, God is invited to consider "His entrails" — His natural mercy.
H4578.origine: The Hebrew word מֵעֶה (meeh) designates the interior of the body, the intra-corporeal. It is related to the notion of what is within, hidden in the depths of the body. It is a concrete word that, like many terms designating physical organs in the Bible, has taken on emotional and moral meaning: the Hebrews located deep feelings in the belly and entrails, much more than in the heart according to our modern thinking. The word appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, always to speak of what is internal, physically or metaphorically.
H4578.emploi: The word "entrails" appears in the Hebrew Bible about 30 times, particularly in narrative and poetic texts. In family narratives (Genesis, Samuel, Chronicles), it often refers to descendants: one who "comes from the entrails" is a child, a promised descendant. Thus in Genesis 15:4, Abram hears that his heir will be of his own flesh. In passages of illness (2 Chronicles 21), it describes troubles of the internal organs. But above all, in poetry and laments (Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations), the word becomes very rich: it designates the home of emotions — sorrow, compassion, anguish, love. In Lamentations 2:11, the entrails that "boil" express extreme pain. In Isaiah 63:15, God is asked to show His "entrails" (His tenderness). This dual dimension, physical and affective, enriches the biblical text: the whole body participates in the emotions of the soul.
H4578.portee: The word "entrails" reminds us that, for the Bible, we are not disembodied souls: our whole body, down to the deep organs, is the seat of our emotions, our compassion, and our anguish. When the psalmist or the prophet speaks of their entrails, they are not engaging in abstract poetry, but confessing their solidarity with the suffering of the people. God Himself, in the Bible, has "entrails" — a visceral, concrete, embodied tenderness towards His people. This invites us to a compassion that engages the whole body, not just the mind.

sens: tiny particle of sand
innumerable multitude
H4579.detail:
1. Grain of sand: the smallest visible particle of sand. In Isaiah 48:19, the prophet mentions "grains of sand" to illustrate the extreme smallness of each grain considered in isolation.
2. Innumerable multitude: by extension, "grains of sand" denote a quantity so great that it cannot be counted. The text in Isaiah uses this image to promise a descendant as numerous as the grains of sand on the shore — a language that is found in the promises made to Abraham.
H4579.origine: The Hebrew word מָעָה (meah) literally designates a grain or a very fine particle. It comes from a root expressing the idea of being small, fine, thin. This image of the extreme fineness of sand made it a natural symbol of what is innumerable, since one cannot count the countless grains that make up a beach.
H4579.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 48:19. The prophet uses it to express the immensity of a promised descendant: the "fruits of your entrails" will be "like the grains of sand." This image recalls a classic motif of fertility promises (see Genesis 22:17 which promises a descendant "like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore"). The word remains anchored in the language of divine blessing.
H4579.portee: This image reminds us that God measures blessing not in countable units, but in elusive abundance. It invites the believer to recognize that God's faithfulness produces fruits that exceed any enumeration — whether it be a descendant, a work, or a grace received. It is a word of hope for those who doubt that God can fulfill His promises.

sens: bread or cake baked, a staple food prepared with flour and oil
a person who mocks or enjoys ridiculing, particularly in a malicious manner
H4580.detail:
1. The word refers to a food prepared from flour, generally baked in an oven or on a hot stone — it is a simple bread or cake, common food in ancient Israel. The widow of Zarephath in 1 Kings 17:12 mentions this modest dish: she has only a handful of flour and a little oil to make this "baked food" before dying of hunger with her son.
2. The word takes on a figurative meaning, that of a light, mocking, or disdainful person — someone who enjoys ridiculing and making fun. In Psalms 35:16, the "mocking parasites" are those who gnash their teeth and laugh at the psalmist with contempt; the name perhaps evokes the hollow, insubstantial nature of mockery, or the way these mockers gravitate around their victim like parasites.
H4580.origine: The Hebrew root עוג (ʿwg) means "to form a ball" or "to round," which explains why the word designates a shaped and baked food. This image of a rounded or ball shape has figuratively extended to the notion of someone insignificant or bothersome — a "parasite" who hovers around others. The connection between the food and the mocking person may seem strange, but it reflects a common Hebrew wordplay: the same word changes meaning according to context.
H4580.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, with two distinct meanings. In 1 Kings 17:12, it describes a concrete food, the cake or baked bread that the widow wants to prepare in famine. In Psalms 35:16, in parallel with "wicked" and "mockers," it designates people who mock — the idea of derision and contempt is present. These two uses show how biblical Hebrew could attach multiple meanings to the same word depending on context, a semantic richness that requires particular attention from the reader.
H4580.portee: For the Christian, the first meaning recalls the widow's trust in the God who provides, even in extreme poverty: she prepares her last meal with the intention of sharing it with the prophet, an act of faith that will be rewarded by a miracle. The second meaning warns us against the lightness of those who mock the people of God: a parasitic attitude that gnaws and belittles is contrary to love and respect for others.

sens: Fortified building, naturally or artificially defended place where one resists enemies
Refuge, asylum where one finds safety
Strength, power that protects and supports
Divine support that guarantees salvation
H4581.detail:
1. A fortress is primarily a real place, built or natural, where one defends oneself: a steep rock, thick walls, a location that withstands attack. This is why the psalmist says, "Be my rock of refuge, a fortress" (Psalms 31:3) — he asks God for true physical protection in his persecutions.
2. But the word also designates, more broadly, any refuge where one escapes from threat. Jeremiah cries, "O Lord, my strength and my fortress" (Jeremiah 16:19), emphasizing what shelters and welcomes us when everything collapses.
3. The word can mean strength itself, the active power that protects us. David sings, "God is my strength" (2 Samuel 22:33 in the list of references), and it is this living power that defends us.
4. Finally, it denotes the divine support that saves and keeps us: not a wall of stone, but the certainty that God supports us and guarantees us victory. This is the most spiritual meaning and the one most cherished by the psalmists.
H4581.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be strong, to be hard." The basic image is that of rock, of hard mineral that does not yield. Related terms include: "oz" (strength), "azaz" (to strengthen oneself). In Aramaic, the word also takes on this sense of power and refuge. In the Greek Bible, this word is often translated by terms that express strength, solidity, and security.
H4581.emploi: This word appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms (13 times) where the faithful invoke God as their fortress, and in the Prophets. In the Psalms, it almost always describes divine refuge: the psalmist asks God to be his fortress when the enemy pursues him. In Isaiah, the word takes on a political hue: cities and kingdoms have their fortresses (Isaiah 17:9, 23:4). In Daniel, it speaks of the military power that supports kings (Daniel 11:1, 11:31). In all cases, the word designates what is hard, solid, impregnable — whether it be stone walls or divine strength.
H4581.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that God is not distant or weak, but a present, tangible, unshakeable strength. It is an invitation to stop seeking our security in human alliances, money, or power, and to rely on Him who cannot falter. Whenever life threatens or terrifies us, the word "fortress" reminds us that we have access to absolute solidity, a living protection that holds us.

sens: father of King Achish of Gath
H4582.detail: Maoc is a character from the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is the father of Achish, king of Gath, and appears only once in biblical history (1 Samuel 27:2), when David flees from King Saul and seeks refuge with Achish son of Maoc in Gath, a city of the Philistines.
H4582.origine: The name Maoc (מָעוֹךְ) means "oppression" in Hebrew. It is a Semitic proper name, with a variant spelling found in the same Bible: Maacah (מַעֲכָה). The etymology evokes the idea of pressing, crushing — a classic image of domination or suffering in Hebrew culture.
H4582.emploi: Maoc is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 27:2. He is simply identified as the father of King Achish of Gath, where David finds refuge with his six hundred men during his flight from Saul. He is a minor character in the story, mentioned only to establish Achish's genealogy and situate him in the political context of Gath during the days of the united monarchy.

sens: Place of residence, house or lodging
Refuge, place of protection and safety
Den or lair of wild animals
Heavenly dwelling of God
Retreat, secluded place
H4583.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a place where one lives, a house or lodging. It is the home, the domicile where one regularly lives: when speaking of God's "holy dwelling" in the heavens, one imagines His heavenly habitation (Deuteronomy 26:15).
2. The word can also mean a refuge, an asylum, a place where one is sheltered from danger and feels protected. The psalmist says to the Lord: "You make the Most High your dwelling" (Psalms 91:9), thus expressing the sense of security found in God.
3. The word also applies to the den or lair of wild beasts — for example, the lair of lions from which they cannot be disturbed (Nahum 2:12), or the burrows that jackals dig to shelter themselves.
4. When it comes to God, the word takes on a majestic dimension: His "holy dwelling" refers to heaven, the place where He resides in His holiness and glory, from which He observes the earth and intervenes (Jeremiah 25:30).
5. The word can finally evoke a retreat, a secluded place where one isolates oneself — a nuance that emphasizes the out-of-the-way, hidden nature of this place.
H4583.origine: The Hebrew word מָעוֹן comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to bend" or "to take refuge," like someone curling up to shelter themselves. This root suggests the image of a cave or a hollow place where one can slip in. The word belongs to the family of terms designating a refuge, an asylum, and appears mainly in the Psalms and the prophets to speak of rest and protection.
H4583.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Psalms, among the prophets (Jeremiah, Nahum, Zephaniah), and in the historical books. It is first used to evoke God's dwelling in heaven, as in the blessing of Israel given by Moses (Deuteronomy 26:15) or in Jeremiah's prayer where he sees God roaring from His holy dwelling (Jeremiah 25:30). The Psalms use it to express divine protection: the refugee finds in God a safe "retreat" (Psalms 91:9). The word also designates the den of wild animals, particularly lions (Nahum 2:12), and the burrows of animals that desert a land become desolate (Jeremiah 9:11, 10:22). In all these contexts, the word evokes both the solidity of the refuge and the idea of retreating away from turmoil.
H4583.portee: This word reminds believers that God has a dwelling place — heaven — from which He reigns and blesses His people. It also invites the faithful to see in God their own spiritual dwelling, their assured refuge in the face of life's threats and anxieties. The image of the "dwelling" emphasizes that our relationship with God is not fleeting, but anchored, stable, like a home.

sens: City of Judah located about thirteen kilometers south of Hebron
Desert region surrounding this city, place of refuge
People or ethnicity of the Maonites mentioned in the history of the oppressors of Israel
H4584G.detail: 1. Maon is a city in southern Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:55). It was located near other localities such as Carmel and Ziph. 2. The region surrounding the city, called the desert of Maon, served as a refuge for David fleeing Saul; several times the texts report that David and his men hid there and that Saul pursued them (1 Samuel 23:24-25). 3. The Maonites are among the peoples who oppressed Israel during the time of the Judges, before the people cried out to God for deliverance (Judges 10:12).
H4584G.origine: The name Maon literally means "habitation" in Hebrew. The city bears this generic name, like many places in the land of Israel. It existed as an inhabited locality during the conquest and division of the territory under Joshua.
H4584G.emploi: Maon appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first mentioned as one of the cities of Judah (Joshua 15:55). During the time of the Judges, the Maonites are cited among the enemies of Israel who oppressed it (Judges 10:12). Most of the uses concern the period of David in flight: the desert of Maon becomes a key location in his wanderings, where Saul tracks him several times (1 Samuel 23:24-25). One of these passages also mentions a wealthy man from Maon who had large flocks (1 Samuel 25:2), suggesting that the region was fertile and inhabited.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
City in southern Judah, about 13 kilometers south of Hebron
H4584H.detail:
1. Maon is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shammai, mentioned only once in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:45). His name means "habitation" or "dwelling." 
2. Maon also refers to a city in Judah, located about 13 kilometers south of Hebron. This city gave its name to its inhabitants, the Maonites. David took refuge there for a time during his flight from Saul.
H4584H.origine: The name Maon comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dwell" or "to stay"; it evokes the idea of a dwelling or a refuge. The word expresses the image of a place where one resides, which is why it is used both for a man (the bearer of this name) and for a inhabited place (the city).
H4584H.emploi: Maon appears as a man in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:45, where he is presented as the son of Shammai. The same name also designates a city in southern Judah, home to a community (the Maonites). This duality of meaning — a man and a place — reflects a common usage in the Bible, where place names can also designate ancestors or founders.

sens: Underground refuge or cavity where wild animals hide
Usual den or lair of a beast
Dwelling or habitation (in a literal or figurative sense)
Place of strength or security (for a person, a city)
H4585.detail:
1. The den is primarily the underground refuge or natural cavity where animals hide: "The wild animal retreats into a cave, and lies down in its den" (Job 37:8). It is the lair of the lion, the leopard, and any predator that sleeps and rests safely.
2. By extension, it is the usual lair, the territory where the animal hunts and lives: "When they lie down in their den, when they lie in ambush in their lair" (Job 39:2). The word designates the living and action place of the beast.
3. The Bible also uses it for a human dwelling, a proper habitation: "His tent is in Salem, and his dwelling is in Zion" (Psalms 76:3). Here the word rises: it speaks of the place where God dwells among His people.
4. Finally, it becomes a symbol of strength and protection: Jerusalem boasts of its "dwellings" (Jeremiah 21:13) as fortresses from which no one can expel it. It is a place where one feels impregnable.
H4585.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root עון (ôn), which evokes the idea of curling up, of taking refuge by hiding. This root also produces related terms to designate misfortune or danger — the central idea is that of vulnerability seeking shelter. The den is literally the place where a creature curls up to escape danger.
H4585.emploi: The word den appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Poetic and Prophetic books. In Job and the Psalms, it first designates the refuges of animals: lion, leopard, wild beasts — God sees them in their dens (Psalms 104:22). The Song of Songs poetically mentions it: "from the dens of lions" (Song of Songs 4:8). But the word also extends to humans: Jeremiah uses it for the fortified "dwellings" of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 21:13), and Nahum for the lair of Nineveh (Nahum 2:13). In each case, the word retains the idea of a protected, secret place from which one observes without being seen.
H4585.portee: This word reminds us that every living being, from the lion to man, seeks a refuge, a safe place to exist. For the believer, it evokes the promise that God is our refuge and fortress (Deuteronomy 33:27 in thematic parallel) — the only truly inviolable shelter. It also reminds us that sin needs to hide and that our true dwellings are not these fortresses of pride, but the trust in the One who knows us everywhere.

sens: People living in southern Canaan during the time of the kings of Judah
Group of exiles who returned, possibly descendants of the people mentioned above
H4586G.detail:
1. The Maonites are a people who lived in the regions south of Canaan. In 1 Chronicles 4:41, during the time of King Hezekiah, men of Judah attacked them, destroyed their tents, and settled in their place for the grazing of their flocks.
2. The name of the Maonites reappears in 2 Chronicles 26:7 as enemies of King Uzziah: God helps him against them, alongside the Philistines and the Arabs of Gur-Baal. It is possible that some of them returned from exile and settled in Judah.
H4586G.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew word meaning "dwellings" or "habitations." It designates a people whose precise origin is unknown, but who occupied the southern part of the land of Canaan and the surrounding desert. These inhabitants, possibly originating from a region called Maon or Meunite, are known only from these two biblical mentions.
H4586G.emploi: The Maonites appear only twice in the Bible, both times in Chronicles. First in 1 Chronicles 4:41, where King Hezekiah and his warriors defeat them, destroy their encampments, and take their lands. Then in 2 Chronicles 26:7, where King Uzziah successfully confronts them, aided by God. In both cases, they are enemies of the kingdom of Judah who are repelled or subdued to conquer lands and pastures.

sens: Group of exiles returning from Babylon appearing in the return lists
People or clan whose descendants belong to the temple servants during the return from exile
H4586H.detail:
1. The Mehunim are mentioned in the lists of those returning from Babylon after the captivity. Ezra 2:50 and Nehemiah 7:52 enumerate them among the sons (descendants) of various families, indicating that they formed a group identified with its own ancestors.
2. Their place in these enumerations suggests that they belonged to the group of temple servants (the Nethinim), these non-Israelites who performed the humblest manual tasks of worship. This indicates a specific social condition and an established role in the returning community.
H4586H.origine: The name Mehunim or Mehun could mean "dwellings" or be related to an ancestor whose memory has been preserved in the people's memory. Few details remain about the precise origin of this group, but its name appears mainly in the genealogical lists of the post-exilic period, reflecting the importance that these records had in establishing identity and status within the restored community.
H4586H.emploi: The Mehunim appear only twice in the Bible, both times in the return lists from exile: Ezra 2:50 and Nehemiah 7:52. These two passages are very close and are part of the official lists of the people returning from Babylonian captivity under the leadership of Zerubbabel. They are systematically listed alongside other groups (Asna, Nephusim, Besaï, Nephischsim), indicating that they constituted a recognizable administrative and social entity. Their presence in these two parallel texts underscores their stable place in the hierarchy of the returning community.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, living before the monarchy in Israel
H4587.detail: Meonothaï is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the genealogy of Judah. He is the son of Othniel and the father of Ophra (1 Chronicles 4:14). His name means "my dwellings" in Hebrew, evoking the establishment of a family in a place of residence. He appears in the list of descendants of Kenaz, an important ancestor of the tribe of Judah.
H4587.origine: The name Meonothaï (מְעוֹנֹתַי) comes from the Hebrew "méon" which means "dwelling" or "habitation," with a possessive suffix "-ay" meaning "my." The full name thus expresses "my habitations" or "my dwellings." This type of name reflects the importance of stability and territorial establishment for Israelite families.
H4587.emploi: Meonothaï appears only twice in the Bible, both in the genealogical passage of 1 Chronicles 4:13-14. He is presented as the son of Othniel and the father of Ophra. These two verses constitute the only biblical mention of this character, who is part of the long genealogy of the tribe of Judah before the establishment of the monarchy in Israel. His role is purely genealogical, serving to establish the family ties between the ancient leaders and the descendants of Kenaz.

sens: To plunge into darkness, shadow, or blackness
To be engulfed in distress and turmoil
H4588.detail:
1. The word literally describes the act of tipping over, sinking into darkness or shadow — an image of light going out or clarity disappearing. In Isaiah 8:22, the prophet speaks of "dark anxieties" that envelop a man deprived of God's help: it is a complete obscuration, a thick darkness where nothing can be seen.
2. Figuratively, to sink denotes the state of one who is immersed in moral distress, turmoil, and misfortune — as if an inner night covers the soul. The context of Isaiah shows that this sinking into darkness accompanies the rejection of God's word: it results in total obscurity, without hope, without light.
H4588.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of being covered, enveloped, closed — like something plunged into shadow or covered in darkness. This same family of words appears in other biblical contexts to describe what is veiled, hidden, or inaccessible to light. The image is that of day sinking into night — a tipping into darkness and invisibility.
H4588.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 8:22. It fits into an apocalyptic description where the prophet shows the fate of those who refuse to consult God and His Word: instead of finding refuge in the Law and the Testimony, they find themselves plunged into a triple darkness — distress, thick darkness — deprived of all light. The unique but powerful usage underscores the irreversibility of this sinking: one who rejects God tips without recourse into a chasm of darkness.
H4588.portee: This word highlights a crucial truth: the rejection of God is not a neutral matter — it plunges us into a tangible moral and spiritual darkness. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that the Word of God is the source of light and guidance in life; without it, we sink. Conversely, it is an invitation to seek clarity and hope in God in the face of distress.

sens: The state of one who is without clothing, completely naked
Figuratively: shame, dishonor, or what one seeks to hide
H4589.detail:
1. Nakedness is the state of the body without clothing. In Habakkuk 2:15, the prophet denounces one who intoxicates his neighbor to see his nakedness: it is an act of mockery and vileness, a violation of the respect owed to others. Nakedness exposes the body and confers a kind of vulnerability or shame.
2. In figurative language, this word can denote shame or dishonor itself, or what one wishes to keep hidden — moral nakedness, weakness, or guilt that one conceals from others. The context of the verse in Habakkuk shows that seeing someone's nakedness is a form of humiliation.
H4589.origine: The Hebrew word מָעוֹר (maor) comes from a root that expresses the idea of denudation or exposure. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that describe the unclothed body, in contrast to one who wears clothing. This term appears rarely in biblical Hebrew, reflecting the sacred nature of the body and the seriousness of nakedness in biblical culture.
H4589.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 2:15. In this passage, the prophet pronounces judgment against one who seeks to give his neighbor an intoxicating drink to see him naked — an image of degradation and contempt. This unique usage underscores the sinful and humiliating dimension of the act: it is never an innocent nakedness, but always an exposure of shame or a violation of respect.
H4589.portee: This word reminds us that the body must be respected, and that seeking to expose or humiliate others is a grave sin. It also invites the reader to guard their own honor and that of others, refusing mockery and acts that degrade. For Habakkuk, it is a warning: God sees all our actions, even the most hidden or shameful.

sens: Priest of the temple service during the time of David
H4590G.detail: Maaziah is a priest mentioned in the text of 1 Chronicles 24, which lists the twenty-four divisions (or "courses") of the priestly service established by David. Maaziah led the twenty-fourth and last of these courses (1 Chronicles 24:18), meaning that he and his family took turns performing the ritual service at the temple for one week each year. It was a role of responsibility and honor in the worship of Israel.
H4590G.origine: The name Maaziah means "Yahweh's consolation" in Hebrew. It is composed of maa ("refuge, shelter") and yah ("Yahweh"), thus expressing the idea that God is a consolation and shelter for His people.
H4590G.emploi: Maaziah appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:18, in the list of leaders of the twenty-four priestly courses established by King David. This organization, somewhat later in its writing, reflects the functioning of temple worship in Jerusalem. The text provides no further details about this priest: his role is limited to his name and rank in the hierarchical order of the cultic service.

sens: Priest during the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem
H4590H.detail: Maaziah is a priest mentioned in the book of Nehemiah, at the time when the Israelites return from exile in Babylon and rebuild Jerusalem. His name means "Jehovah's consolation." In Nehemiah 10:8, he is listed among the priests who affix their seal to the solemn covenant by which the people commit to obey God's Law after the return. He is a man of faith, a spiritual leader who publicly seals his people's covenant with the Lord.
H4590H.origine: The name Maaziah comes from Hebrew: it is composed of two elements — "ma" (of) and "aziah" (consolation/divine strength), forming a theophoric name that expresses the consolation that God brings. This type of name was common among priests and spiritual leaders of Israel to express trust in divine protection.
H4590H.emploi: Maaziah appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:8, among the priests and Levites who sign the covenant of Nehemiah. He represents one of the priestly families of the Return, tasked with maintaining worship and fidelity to the Law in restored Jerusalem. The text presents him alongside other priests of rank, highlighting his authority and role in the spiritual leadership of the rebuilding community.

sens: To become less great, fewer, less important
To reduce in quantity, number, or value
To weaken, weakening (especially in terms of age or strength)
H4591.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses the simple idea of becoming small or few: a house is "too few" to accommodate a whole lamb (Exodus 12:4), or the quantities of manna vary — the one who gathered the least still had ten homers (Numbers 11:32). It is to observe that something has been reduced.
2. The meaning extends to the action of voluntarily reducing: in the division of the Levitical cities, those who have less give "in fewer numbers" (Numbers 35:8), or the poor shall not "pay less" tax than another (Exodus 30:15). It is to make something small.
3. The word can also describe the natural weakening of the body or strength: in Ecclesiastes 12:5, those who grind cease because they are "diminished," an image of aging that takes away vigor. Similarly, livestock should not be "diminished" by punishment (Psalms 107:38).
H4591.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root denoting the state of being small or few (hence the name מְעַט, "few"). The underlying image is one of reduction, of contraction: something that occupied more space, had more value or strength, loses it. The verb conjugates in several forms that deepen the idea: to become small oneself, or to make small, to give less.
H4591.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in the Psalms and Prophets. It primarily designates concrete realities: the number of people, cities, livestock, the quantities of tax or plunder. Gradually, it also applies to the abstract: to "diminish" the number of the living (Leviticus 26:22 — divine punishment), to "diminish" a nation (Ezekiel 29:15), or to "diminish" a punishment so that it is not too severe (Jeremiah 10:24). The usage shows that the word covers both natural reduction and voluntary or providential reduction.
H4591.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the finitude and reductions that life brings: aging, poverty, diminishing strength. But it also shows that God controls reductions: He can limit them ("do not diminish their livestock") or proportion them to each person's capacity. It is a subtle lesson on acceptance and providence.

sens: a small quantity or a small number
a brief duration, a moment
insufficient, too little
almost, just, barely
H4592.detail:
1. A small quantity or a small number: the word designates what is reduced in volume, number, or importance. When Abram asks for "a little water" (Genesis 18:4), it refers to a modest but sufficient amount for an immediate need. Similarly, Jonathan tastes "a little" honey (1 Samuel 14:29) — a mere drop, but enough to revive his strength. The context of lots drawn shows its use in the sense of "small portion" (Numbers 26:54).
2. A brief duration, a moment: the word expresses the shortness of time. "Yet a little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field" (Isaiah 29:17) announces an imminent change. Job cries: "Are not my days few?" (Job 10:20), emphasizing the brevity of human life in the face of eternity.
3. Insufficient, too little: the emphasis is then on inadequacy or lack. Korah protests: "Is it not enough that you have brought us out...?" (Numbers 16:13) — the word expresses the idea that what has been given is not sufficient for the rebellions that arise from it.
4. Almost, barely, just: sometimes the word brushes against the meaning of a quasi-reality. "A little sleep, a little slumber" (Proverbs 6:10) describes fleeting moments where laziness gains ground. It is the image of time slipping away imperceptibly.
H4592.origine: The Hebrew word מְעַט (me.at) comes from a root expressing the idea of "tiny" or "reduced." Its primary image is that of something small, thin, poor in substance. It is found in compounds and derivatives designating smallness or insufficiency. The Old Testament uses it to contrast the humility of God's people with the grand promises made to them.
H4592.emploi: The word appears 92 times in biblical Hebrew, particularly in the Torah (Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its primary meaning is quantitative: a small amount of food or water (Genesis 18:4), a small number of people (Deuteronomy 7:7: Israel is "the least of all peoples"), a meager harvest (Deuteronomy 28:38). The word easily glides towards the temporal: a few days or a moment (Isaiah 10:25, 26:20). It can also express insufficiency or reproach (Numbers 16:13). Finally, in a context of promise or hope, it emphasizes the imminence or immanence of an event that is coming soon (Isaiah 29:17). Its usage reflects the biblical tension between the smallness of Israel and the vastness of God's plans.
H4592.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the greatness of God in the face of human fragility: Israel is "few," but God chooses and blesses it (Deuteronomy 7:7). It also teaches sobriety: Proverbs values "little" with integrity rather than "much" obtained through dishonesty (Proverbs 15:16, 16:8). Finally, it reminds that life is short (Job 10:20), urging not to postpone what truly matters to God.

sens: having a sharp edge, pointed
shining with a bright luster
prepared, sharpened to do harm
H4593.detail: 1. The word first designates what has a sharp edge: a sharpened sword is a sword whose blade has been prepared, sharpened to cut cleanly. 2. The image is enriched with a nuance of brightness and shine: a sharpened sword sparkles, it shines in a threatening way. 3. In a figurative sense, this means being ready, prepared, intended for a deadly purpose — the sword is not only sharpened materially, it is armed with malicious intent (Ezekiel 21:20: "it is sharpened for slaughter").
H4593.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of piercing, pointing, making sharp. The basic meaning is mechanical: the result of a blade being honed against a stone or steel, becoming sharp and shiny. It is a concrete term, related to tools and weapons.
H4593.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the dramatic context of Ezekiel 21, where the prophet describes the sword of God's judgment. It is both sharpened (ready to strike), shining (terrifying to behold), and formidable (intended for slaughter). The unique usage concentrates all the intensity of the divine threat.
H4593.portee: This term reminds us that divine justice is neither abstract nor soft: God's sword is sharpened, ready, effective. For the believer, it is a warning about the reality of judgment; for the one who repents, it is a call to take the prophetic word seriously.

sens: Coat or covering that wraps the body
Image of a spiritual covering or adornment given by God
H4594.detail:
1. The word refers to a garment that envelops, a coat: something that covers and protects the body (Isaiah 61:3).
2. Figuratively, it represents a spiritual covering or a moral adornment that God grants to His children, like a new dignity: thus the prophet speaks of a "garment of praise" given to the afflicted to replace their despair and mourning (Isaiah 61:3).
H4594.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to wrap" or "to cover." It evokes the primary image of a fabric or coat that wraps around someone. In Hebrew, several terms designate clothing according to their function or form; this one particularly emphasizes the idea of covering and protecting.
H4594.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 61:3). It is used poetically and metaphorically to describe the "garment of praise" that the Lord bestows upon the afflicted in exchange for their downcast spirit. This image emphasizes that divine consolation is not merely an inner word: it is a visible "adornment," a new dignity that envelops the one who receives it.
H4594.portee: This garment of praise reminds the believer that the joy and confidence granted by God are not hidden deep in the heart: they are worn publicly, like a new dignity that radiates outward. For those who suffer or are downcast, this word invites belief that God desires not only to console but also to restore the dignity and beauty of those He loves.

sens: Loose garment worn over the ordinary tunic
Luxury garment worn by wealthy women
H4595.detail:
1. The loose tunic is a roomy garment, an outer tunic that is worn over the basic tunic. It is an additional element of the outfit, intended to add volume and majesty to the silhouette. In Isaiah 3:22, it is listed among the precious ornaments of women, alongside coats and purses.

2. This garment was a luxury item, primarily worn by women of high society and aristocracy. Its "loose" and generous character indicates that it was a symbol of wealth and social status: only affluent women could afford this additional adornment.
H4595.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of wrapping or covering. The loose tunic is literally what "envelops": it covers and dresses the body. It is part of the family of Hebrew terms designating clothing and adornments.
H4595.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 3:22. The prophet lists the luxurious ornaments and garments that the proud women of Jerusalem wore: large tunics, coats, purses, mirrors, etc. This passage places the loose tunic in a context of prophetic critique against the ostentation and vanity of the wealthy women of Jerusalem.
H4595.portee: This garment reminds us that external adornment and luxury attract divine judgment when they become signs of pride and distance from God. The mention of these beautiful garments in the prophet's words invites the reader to reflect on what truly deserves our attachment: not fleeting beauty, but wisdom and the fear of the Lord.

sens: A pile, a mound of debris
The state of a city completely destroyed
H4596.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a heap or pile — here, a mound of stones and debris. In Isaiah 17:1, Damascus, a great city, will be nothing but a "heap" of ruins: an image of total destruction where only piled stones remain, no structure standing.
2. Figuratively, it represents the end of a city: from the radiance and urban life, only a chaotic mound will remain, a symbol of divine judgment that annihilates human pride.
H4596.origine: The Hebrew word מְעִי (me.i) fundamentally means "a heap" or "a pile." It evokes the idea of something stacked, accumulated without order. This root belongs to the vocabulary of destruction and ruin, common in the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah that depict the collapse of rebellious cities.
H4596.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 17:1. It is used in a prophetic word announcing the fall of Damascus, the capital of Syria. This context is one of divine judgment upon the nations: a powerful city, a place of life and activity, will become a mere heap — a spectacular image of total annihilation.
H4596.portee: This word reminds us of the reality of divine judgment upon the pride of empires. It also shows that nothing built by man against the Lord can endure: even the greatest city remains only a heap of forgotten debris. It is an invitation to place one's hope not on human strength, but on God alone.

sens: Levite musician from the time of the return from exile
H4597.detail: Maai is a Levite musician, son of Asaph, who participated in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile. He appears in a list of musicians accompanying Ezra the scribe during this solemn ceremony (Nehemiah 12:36), where he played musical instruments belonging to David.
H4597.origine: The name Maai means "compassionate" or "merciful" in Hebrew. It is part of the Levitical family of Asaph, a large family of musicians and singers of the Temple. The context of his appearance in Scripture places him at the heart of Israel's return from exile and the restoration of Temple worship.
H4597.emploi: Maai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:36. He is part of an impressive brotherhood of Levite musicians (his brothers are Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Guilalai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani). All participated together in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, a major event marking the restoration of the religious and communal life of Israel returned from Babylonian captivity. This unique mention shows him as a humble servant of divine worship, one of the many Levites who contributed to reestablishing the service of the Temple.

sens: Loose and long garment worn over others, sign of dignity or high rank
Ceremonial robe of the high priest of Israel
Distinctive garment worn by the king's daughters
(Figuratively) Attribute or quality that someone puts on
H4598.detail:
1. It is a loose and long garment that is worn over a tunic or shirt. High-ranking men — princes, kings — wore this mantle to show their dignity and power. Saul wears it and gives it to David as a sign of favor (1 Samuel 18:4). It is a garment that can be removed or torn as a sign of mourning or shame, as Job does upon learning of his misfortune (Job 1:20).
2. The high priest of Israel wore a special robe, blue in color, made entirely of fine fabric (Exodus 39:22). This robe was adorned with bells and pomegranates all around its hem (Exodus 39:26); it was a sacred garment, reserved for worship and a sign of his religious authority.
3. Among the king's daughters, the mantle was a distinctive garment that marked their status. David's daughter, Tamar, wore a multicolored tunic, a garment worn as long as she was a virgin (2 Samuel 13:18), that is, as long as she was unmarried.
4. The word can also figuratively refer to the qualities or attributes of a person — particularly justice, wisdom, or glory — that they put on like a mantle (Isaiah 59:17; Job 29:14).
H4598.origine: The Hebrew word מְעִיל (meïl) refers to a long and loose garment that envelops the body. The basic image is that of something that covers and surrounds. The word belongs to a small Hebrew family concerning clothing; it has an ancient history and remains associated throughout the Old Testament with the idea of dignity, authority, and solemn covering.
H4598.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the Old Testament, mainly in texts related to worship (Exodus, Leviticus) and the history of kings and the righteous (Samuel, Chronicles, Job). In Exodus, it describes the blue linen mantle of the high priest (Exodus 39:22-26). In the accounts of 1 Samuel, it becomes a sign of royal or princely status: Saul gives it to David, and Saul shows it to Samuel when he recognizes him (1 Samuel 15:27; 28:14). In situations of mourning or repentance, the mantle is torn or removed (Job 1:20; Ezra 9:3). Figuratively, it becomes the image of what one is morally or spiritually clothed with (Isaiah 59:17; 61:10; Job 29:14).
H4598.portee: This word reminds us that clothing in the Bible is never neutral: it speaks of rank, responsibility, honor, or, conversely, shame and mourning. For the high priest, the mantle is a constant call to holiness: every bell that rings is an audible presence before God. Figuratively, the mantle invites us to reflect on what truly clothes us — not the outward appearances, but the moral and spiritual qualities we cultivate.

sens: Opening in the ground from which water naturally flows
Water that springs from a source
Fertile or rich place that produces abundantly
Origin, principle from which something derives
H4599.detail:
1. A spring is the point where water naturally emerges from the ground, usually in mountainous or rocky areas. It is the place where underground water rises to the surface and begins to flow. In Genesis 7:11, during the Flood, "all the springs of the great deep burst forth": these massive underground springs opened all at once.
2. The word also refers to the water itself that springs from this point. When one speaks of stopping up a spring (2 Kings 3:19), they are preventing the water from flowing to deprive the enemy of drink.
3. By extension, a spring becomes an image of what is fertile, living, and abundant. Proverbs 5:16 speaks of the springs of one who has received wisdom, as if wisdom naturally and generously flows from them, able to quench the thirst of many.
4. Finally, the word evokes the origin or the primary cause from which something proceeds. When Proverbs 8:24 speaks of the absence of springs before creation, it is the image of what does not yet exist, before anything bursts forth.
H4599.origine: The Hebrew word מַעְיָן comes from a root that denotes the bursting forth, the emergence. It is related to the idea of something that comes out, that springs forth with force. The word evokes the very action of water rising and rushing out of the ground. In biblical Hebrew, this word is used in contexts where water naturally emerges, often in an abundant and powerful manner.
H4599.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and wisdom literature. It first refers to real, geographical springs of water: those of the Flood (Genesis 7:11), the springs that King Hezekiah closed to starve the enemy (2 Chronicles 32:4), the springs that God dried up or made burst forth as a sign of power (Psalms 74:15, 114:8). It is also used for territorial boundaries marked by a spring (Joshua 15:9). Finally, biblical wisdom uses it figuratively: springs are the image of what spiritually nourishes (Proverbs 5:16 regarding the fruits of wisdom), or what everything proceeds from before creation (Proverbs 8:24). The word can even refer to the character of one who is a source of life or blessing for others.
H4599.portee: This word invites the believer to see in God the Source of all life and goodness. Just as a spring naturally bursts forth and quenches thirst, God is the one from whom our sustenance, joy, and salvation flow. The spring also evokes a living spiritual life: one who receives from God continues to spring forth to give to others, as in Proverbs 5:16. It is a beautiful image of the transmission of divine grace.
